World.title: Croatian Railway Ambitions Tie in With European Defence Efforts
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatian railway ambitions are closely linked with European defence efforts, as the country’s “decade of the railway” is still not really being felt on the ground by most.

Any reason for the renewal and development of the railway system in Croatia is very useful, including the security and defence one. But its civilian role remains primary. Index/Deutsche Welle/Igor Lasic reports that following two serious railway traffic incidents at the beginning of this month in Croatia, this mode of passenger and freight transport is once again a topic for the Croatian public.

Moreover, the general public has been reminded of the fact that Croatia is apparently currently in the middle of its “decade of the railway”. This is a state project for the development of this long-neglected mode of transport, with an investment of six billion euros for new tracks and vehicles. Yet despite years of reconstruction, the results are still not really visible on the ground, even though some concrete works have long been planned. The announced “railway renaissance” will therefore clearly still have to wait, and the recent traffic accidents have uncomfortably highlighted this uncertainty.

On top of everything, a new element has been included in the reasoning for the renewal of the Croatian railway sector, and that’s the wider European defence system. Europe is rapidly arming itself, and Croatia has also bought, among other things, more than 40 German Leopard 2 tanks. These, however, because of their exceptional weight, require equally exceptional railway transport capacities. All of this ultimately enters into the final calculation of the development project of the public company Croatian Railways. On the other hand, its relative urgency and the need for centralisation of the system somewhat remove the possibility of imminent privatisation of the sector, which until recently was quite realistic.

so long, privatisation

“Only through the security sphere and social cohesion around the issue of defence have we come to the conclusion that the railway must be managed by the state if we want an efficient system,” Ante Klečina, a railway expert and lecturer at the Department of Sustainable Mobility and Logistics of the University Sjever (North) in Koprivnica and Varaždin, told DW. He referred to the experience of some more developed European countries, such as Great Britain, whose experiments with railway privatisation ended rather ignominiously. Services became of poor quality and too expensive, the system failed in various aspects, and over time it was abandoned.

“First and foremost should be their functionality for civilian needs and, in fact, the organisation of civilisation,” Klečina continues, “which is relevant at every moment if we do not put that priority out of our minds. Whoever swears by the advantages of market mechanisms forgets that they are not developmentally suitable for large public systems, those that enable basic requirements.” In his opinion, the same applies to other elementary systems, e.g. healthcare, education and the judiciary, etc. The private sector, says Klečina, can be a supplement in certain segments, but the backbone must remain public.

“The reason is the necessity of central planning of such systems, as well as their primarily non-profit task, but also the need for enormous investments for which private individuals usually have neither the capacity nor the interest. Having seen this in practice, Europe has recently abandoned the idea of privatising railways, and the defence topic came afterwards as an additional reason,” considers Ante Klečina, formerly president of the Railway Alliance in the Republic of Croatia. He further notes that this mode of transport has no equal with regard to a series of key factors: above all overall cost-effectiveness, economic multiplier effects and environmental suitability.

central planning will always be needed

Socioeconomist Toni Prug, for his part, believes that behind the question of Croatian railways lies the general problem of political and scientific rejection of planning and public production as a relic of the past. That past concerns the period of socialism and Yugoslavia, and everything connected with it remained at the very least stigmatised after the war in Croatia. “In reality, however, all successful states are huge public production systems,” says Prug, “in which planning decides on the largest budgets within economies, on interventions whose importance for the population surpasses the importance of decisions that market actors make.”

This assistant professor at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Rijeka highlights the rule in business that when a market actor makes a mistake, i.e. when things go badly, competition replaces him. “And railways, like all other production systems of a public character that are physically fixed and have monopoly status, need to be carefully planned. Mistakes are much harder to correct. They are also managed differently, different parameters are optimised, a focus on profit does not help. It often cannot even be the goal; the goals are determined by the plan.” At the same time the question arises of whether the Republic of Croatia has the professional staff for designing and implementing this.

“private goals have prevailed over practicality”

“Our profession and managerial staff are educated through faculty and professional curricula that say almost nothing about why and how to produce systems and services of a public character, and why they are superior for certain needs,” Prug is convinced, adding that this knowledge still exists in some Croatian public systems, while in others it has collapsed and been left to spontaneity. In his assessment, the City of Zagreb represents a recent example in Croatia that planning can return and capacities be rebuilt. And on higher-quality, data- and analysis-based foundations, which does not concern the railway but can be a general model.

Toni Prug, who in his scientific work has dealt quite a bit with the topic of public sector management, finally conveyed to us the impression that Croatian Railways have so far been a kind of victim of the oil and automobile lobby. “Their private and profit goals have prevailed over the practicality, efficiency, safety and ecological superiority of modern railway systems,” he told DW. Such a hierarchy could change soon thanks to military priorities. But the future of the railway and of social development in general will certainly not be bright if its primarily civilian advantages remain somewhere beside the tracks.

World.title: Croatia Among European Record Holders for Firefighter Numbers
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is among the European record holders when it comes to firefighter numbers as the overall number within Europe has fallen.

Poslovni reports that the total number of firefighters across the EU fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a year that was the worst in EU history in terms of burned area.

Croatia is among the European record holders for firefighter numbers, holding one of the highest shares of professional firefighters in employment in the entire EU. Back in 2025, they accounted for 0.43 percent of total employment, making Croatia second among the 22 EU Member States for which data has been made available. This places Croatia right behind Greece (0.47 percent), according to Euronews. The EU average was 0.18 percent. Portugal follows with 0.33 percent, while the lowest shares are recorded by the Netherlands (0.05), Austria (0.07) and Sweden (0.10 percent).

Across the entire EU there were around 372,400 professional firefighters. Germany had the most, 57,700, followed by France with 47,700 and Italy with 43,500. Next come Poland with 40,000 and Spain with 38,500; the four largest EU economies together account for 187,400 firefighters, or 50.3 percent of the total number. The overall figure in the Union fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a single year that was the worst in EU history for burned areas. The European Trade Union Confederation and EPSU call this drop “reckless cuts” and note that Poland lost 9,000 and France lodt 4,100 firefighters.

Croatia doesn’t rank among the leaders in total numbers, but its share of total employment is among the highest. Eurostat data refers to professional firefighters, including forest firefighters, but not volunteer firefighters. The data also doesn’t show precisely how many professional firefighters are specialised specifically in fighting open-air fires.

The data comes at a time when Europe is facing an ever-growing fire risk. According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) by the 13th of August, the figure had risen to 568,415 hectares from 1,647 fires. For comparison, 2025 was the most destructive season ever recorded in the EU, with 1,079,538 hectares burned in 25 of the 27 EU Member States.

For 2026 the EU has secured a fleet of 22 firefighting aircraft and five helicopters, and in the event of major fires member states can request additional firefighters and equipment through the European Civil Protection Mechanism. In addition, a record 777 firefighters from 14 European countries have been pre-positioned in Cyprus, Greece, Italy, France, Spain and Portugal. Croatia contributes two medium amphibious aircraft to the European fleet, and in 2026 the Commission is also opening a new regional firefighting base in Cyprus with capacity for six aircraft.

World.title: Zadar Was the Most Expensive Croatian City in July
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Zadar was the most expensive Croatian city of all in July, with strong economic growth very much being a double edged sword for the area.

Buying basic groceries has long been a negotiation with one’s own wallet for people in Croatia, but in July, the toughest conditions spilled over onto the area of Zadar County. The basic consumer basket for a four-member family here reached a record 498 euros, reports HRT. Morski writes that a basic daily trip to the shop or the market has become a source of stress for many, and citizens openly complain about the constant quiet price rises:

a previously bustling market sits almost empty

“Vegetables have become very expensive, they get used up quickly, you need a lot of them. Fruit is also very expensive and it seems to me that meat has gone up, fish has also gone up a lot,” says Zadar resident Katja. For pensioners, the situation is even more alarming. Every single purchase requires calculation and a search for discounts: “I really don’t go to the shops much. You buy where you can according to your wallet and that’s it, and yes it’s expensive, it’s definitely expensive, this isn’t for us pensioners, it’s abnormal,” is the honest assessment of Zorica, who lives on the Zagreb–Zadar route.

That consumer habits are changing and that people are buying significantly less than in previous years was confirmed to us by the sellers themselves. Zadar’s market, which in July should be bustling with local and foreign visitors, at times looks unusually empty.

Seller Rada briefly summarises the problem: “Everything is expensive, the shops too.” Her colleague Ilonka points out that even regular customers have thinned out their visits: “There are no customers. I normally have my own customers, but look, two people are walking through the market.”

the price of rapid expansion

How did it come about that Zadar took the top spot for the most expensive groceries? Experts explain that the answer lies in a specific economic effect of the rapid expansion of the regional economy.

Assoc. Prof. Dr. Jurica Bosna, Head of the Department of Economics at the University of Zadar, clarifies the background to this trend: “Nobody wants to have the most expensive basket of goods, but it still shows that the county is developing strongly, and this is an effect known in economics, when we grow faster than we perhaps should according to some optimal economic rates, then it’s unfortunately inevitable that inflation will develop and that the result will be like this,” he stated.

While macroeconomic indicators record the growth and development of the whole of Zadar County, for the general public, that statistic brings no comfort whatsoever. The vicious circle in which the economy advances strongly while prices rise in an unbridled way leaves the deepest mark on household budgets. Since wages and pensions do not come close to keeping pace, the consumer baskets of Zadar residents remain ever emptier.

World.title: Meet the Croatian Road Often Compared to the Legendary Route 66
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – There’s an incredibly scenic Croatian road frequently compared to the legendary Route 66 across the pond in the USA – and a drive along it is nothing less than breathtaking.

When someone mentions Route 66, most people immediately think of the endless American highway, old motels, neon signs and kilometres of asphalt running through some of the most famous landscapes of the United States. Few realise that Croatia has its own very interesting road with the same number in Croatia as well. It goes without saying that Croatia’s D66 doesn’t have thousands of kilometres or hold the status of an American icon, but because of the designation it carries and the landscapes it passes through, it resembles the US legend in many ways.

Putni kofer writes that it has been referred to many times as the Istrian version of Route 66 and presented it as a road that evokes old, nostalgic Istria. Today, the impressive D66 connects Pula, Labin and Vozilići with Opatija, and according to the official decision on the classification of public roads it is about 90 kilometres long. Still, if the goal is to find its most spectacular part, one should head towards the eastern coast of Istria, that is, towards Plomin.

the most impressive section begins at plomin

Plomin is an excellent place to start this short road trip. The old fortified little town sits on a hill above Plomin Bay, and right by the D66 there is also a rest area with a viewpoint. A few kilometres further on there is another spot from which the view opens towards the Kvarner Bay, Cres and Lošinj.

After that begins the stretch that makes it worth driving this road slowly. The asphalt winds under the slopes of Učka, the sea is almost constantly somewhere in sight, and on the other side of the Kvarner Cres appears. In certain places the road runs high enough above the coast that the view feels almost like from a large natural balcony. The greatest advantage of state road D66 is precisely that, over a relatively short distance, viewpoints, medieval places, steep coastline and well-known Kvarner resorts alternate.

the stunning Brseč, a town from 1102 towering above at 157 metres above the sea

SONY DSC

One of the places worth turning off the road for is Brseč. D66 reaches it after driving along the slopes of Učka, and the old part of the settlement is situated on a cliff 157 metres high above the expanse of Kvarner. The first written records of Brseč date back to 1102, although the area was inhabited much earlier. It is particularly interesting that the history of Brseč is also directly linked to the road that passes this way. The Tourist Board of Mošćenička Draga notes that the economic development of the place in the 19th century was spurred by the new road from Pula towards Plomin, then Brseč and Mošćenice and further towards Rijeka.

Today the medieval character of Brseč can still be felt in the narrow streets and passages of the old town core. From the cliff by the little church of St Magdalene one of the most beautiful views in the area opens up, while from the western entrance to the place Cres can be seen. Beneath the high rocks a completely different world is hidden. Between Brseč and Mošćenička Draga lie the beaches of Uboka and Jelenšćica, which can be reached on foot via paths that descend from the main road. The coastline in this area is extremely indented, with steep cliffs, tiny coves and stone fishermen’s cottages by the sea.

from ancient towns to well-known resorts

After Brseč the scenery changes again. D66 continues towards Mošćenička Draga, one of the best-known places at the foot of Učka. The road approaches the sea, and the high rocks gradually give way to beaches and a more built-up coastline. Mošćenička Draga developed from a fishing harbour, and today it is especially known for the long pebble beach of Sipar. Its pebbles were formed by the action of the stream that descends from the slopes of Učka and the sea that has shaped them over the years.

Just a few kilometres further on lies Medveja, another place along the D66 with a long pebble beach. After it comes Lovran, where the whole drive takes on a more elegant appearance. Instead of the almost wild coast around Brseč, old villas, gardens and houses appear along the road that recall the time when this part of the Kvarner became one of the favourite resorts of Central Europe.

just over 90 kilometres from pula to opatija

The entire D66 from Pula to Opatija is a little over 90 kilometres long, but for a panoramic outing the stretch from Plomin to Opatija is especially interesting. According to the kilometres listed on the EuroVelo 8 route, from the Plomin area to Opatija it is roughly thirty kilometres of driving.

That may not sound like much, but that is precisely the charm of this road. In a short drive one passes Plomin Bay, open views towards Cres and Lošinj, medieval Brseč, the steep slopes of Učka, Mošćenička Draga, Medveja, Lovran and finally Opatija. Although it forms part of the Croatian cycling route EuroVelo 8, this road should not be imagined as a lonely carriageway without cars. On the official route website traffic on certain sections is marked as moderate, and from Medveja towards Rijeka as heavy, so if you decide to cover it on four wheels, extra caution is recommended for cyclists.

World.title: Drniš Bypass Construction to Benefit Šibenik Port
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – The future Drniš bypass will greatly benefit the local economy, as well as Šibenik Port directly.

The construction of the second and third phases of the complex Drniš bypass project has begun, with the client being Hrvatske ceste (Croatian roads), and the contractor being the consortium of Texo Molior from Cavtat and CGP Slovenia.

Transport Minister Butković pointed out that after securing the financial structure and signing the contract, work on the project is now starting. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that he also noted that it is a technically complex intervention with a route that includes two overpasses, two viaducts and a bridge over the Čikola River. Speaking about the continuation of activities on the future Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, Minister Butković highlighted that the preparation of project documentation for the section from Drniš towards the Oklaj interchange is in an advanced stage.

a 34 million euro investment

After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, so the project is being gradually prepared for phased implementation. He also referred to the reconstruction of state roads DC56 and DC33, which connect the Drniš area with Split and Knin respectively, and whose total reconstruction value is around 34 million euros. After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, gradually preparing the project for implementation.

“A tender has already been issued for one, the other is in preparation, so there will be a great deal of investment in road infrastructure here in the area of the town of Drniš and Šibenik-Knin County,” added Minister Butković. Šibenik-Knin County Prefect Paško Rakić stressed that the Drniš bypass is of great importance for the entire county, especially for the traffic connection of its hinterland, and that residents of the wider Drniš and Knin areas will use it.

“The Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, as well as this bypass, is the backbone of Šibenik-Knin County in terms of traffic, and it is as important to us as the Pelješac Bridge,” emphasised Prefect Rakić. “This is historic for us,” emphasised Drniš Mayor Tomislav Dželalija, noting that generations of Drniš residents have waited decades for this project.

a massive development boost for the area

Expressing satisfaction that the works were ceremonially started today, he pointed out that the removal of transit traffic, along with increased traffic safety, will create additional preconditions for the expansion of the economic zone and the further development of the town. He added that the Government of the Republic of Croatia, through strong investments including road and railway infrastructure, is giving impetus to the town’s development, and thanked them for the projects being implemented in the Drniš area.

President of the Management Board of Hrvatske ceste Ivica Budimir emphasised that the project has a broader economic significance for Drniš, especially because of the direct connection of the industrial zone with the Šibenik port.

“After this road is constructed, the industrial zone in the entire Drniš area will develop significantly faster, better and to a higher quality, and become much more competitive,” emphasised Budimir. Speaking about the technical demands of the project, he added that almost ten percent of the route consists of viaducts, while the most significant structure is the large bridge over the Čikola River canyon, with a span of 220 metres, along with a series of other structures along the route.

World.title: Baćina Lakes – Meet Croatia’s Freshwater Phenomenon
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Baćina Lakes are Croatia’s freshwater phenomenon, with water warmer than that in the sea and the ability to swim year-round.

If you’ve ever driven from Makarska down toward Dubrovnik, you’ll have passed by them. You probably glanced left for a second, spotted a blue patch amid the greenery, and continued on toward the sea. Yet there, just a few kilometres from Ploče, lies something no other Croatian town has: seven lakes within the boundaries of a single town. They are called the Baćina Lakes and bear names that sound like a list from an old book: Oćuša, Crniševo, Podgora, Sladinac, Šipak, Plitko Lake, and Vrbnik.

Putni kofer writes that six of them are interconnected by narrow passages, so you can paddle or boat from one into another, while Vrbnik, which is also the smallest, is completely separate from the rest. Together they cover about 138 hectares.

they’re warmer than the sea

The Baćina Lakes form a cryptodepression, meaning their surface is only slightly above sea level, while their bottoms lie deep below it. Although they are just a step from the sea and surrounded by permeable limestone, the lakes are freshwater. Some springs are nevertheless directly connected to the sea, so salt water appears in the deeper layers. In the Klokun area near Plitko Lake there is a spring that supplies drinking water to the town of Ploče and the surrounding area.

During the scorching summer, the water in the lakes is noticeably warmer than the sea, with tourist sources citing a difference of roughly three degrees. Because of this, the swimming season here starts earlier and ends later than on the coast. The best-known bathing spots are those near the Mindel spring, and the hidden coves and small beaches are reached by kayak, paddleboard, or traditional Neretva boat.

links with queen teuta

Legend has it that the Illyrian Queen Teuta adored this area, and the lakes are still called Teuta’s pearls. Historians, however, have their own evidence and explanations. Near Sladinac Lake the remains of the Roman settlement of Praetoria have been found, along with the remains of an early Christian basilica from the 6th century and a necropolis of stećci tombstones.

Around the lakes a walking and cycling path about 15 kilometres long has been arranged, with benches, springs, and information boards. In 2020 the Public Institution for Protected Natural Areas of Dubrovnik-Neretva County installed 19 educational boards about dragonflies, amphibians, reptiles, and birds. Near the Oćuša spring there is a bird-watching hide, and the lakes also contain three small islets, one of which is named the Island of Love. The entire area forms part of the Natura 2000 ecological network, within two zones of the Neretva Delta, as a habitat for strictly protected and endemic species.

a worthwhile stop off on a long drive south…

A visit to the Baćina Lakes is truly an experience you will remember for a lifetime. Walking the paths that wind right beside the lakes will reveal scenes covered in water lilies, the reflection of clouds mirrored on the still water, and the song of rare birds that creates an almost meditative atmosphere.

Here you can also swim in crystal-clear water that provides refreshment during the great heat, and a special experience comes when the sun sets and the whole landscape is immersed in golden and pink tones. Then the lakes take on an almost fairy-tale appearance. It is a perfect moment for a photograph, but also for simply enjoying the silence of nature.

In the heart of the summer season, a parking space at the viewpoint along the main road is almost impossible to find. Down by the lakes themselves, however, there are usually no crowds. Most travellers photograph the view and drive on, while those who go down to the water, sit in a boat, or cycle a loop are completely enchanted and, like us, probably think: “How is this place not far better known?”

World.title: Croatia Isn’t Facing a Fuel Shortage, But Prices Will Rise
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Croatia isn’t facing any sort of genuine fuel shortage, but experts are warning that prices will definitely rise.

Diesel shortages aren’t a realistic threat to Croatia, but prices will very likely rise again, warns energy expert Jasminko Umičević. He sees the problem in the lack of refining capacity in Europe and disruptions in supply. Poslovni reports that energy expert Jasminko Umičević spoke about the situation on the energy market, potential shortages and price movements for HRT.

Owing to disruptions on the global oil market and supply problems, concern is growing about the availability of diesel. Energy expert Jasminko Umičević believes there is no real danger of shortages in Croatia, although prices could remain high. “I don’t think there’s any real fear that shortages will occur. I believe high prices will continue, and that is the biggest problem. Regardless of the fact that the diesel market is very tight, especially across Europe. The main reason at this moment is the Strait of Hormuz and all the problems that stem from it,” says Umičević.

He also sees a problem in the structure of European refineries, which do not have sufficient capacity to produce diesel, while Europe has significantly higher consumption of this fuel than, for example, the United States. “European refineries are under-capacitated for sufficient diesel production, because the European market is a diesel market. Today we are in a situation where Europe has reduced its refining capacity by 30 percent over the last 20 years or so. Under the motto: better to import than to produce. And these are the results now,” he stresses. An additional problem for supply is the change in the sources from which Europe obtains all of its diesel.

“Previously the main source was Russia. After the sanctions everything shifted to Arab countries. Now we have a problem with the Arab countries. And recently there have been major problems, after the Ukrainian ones, with the new tactics of destroying refineries. That’s why there is no diesel. The market is tight, it’s always like that – when supply is lower, prices are higher,” he explains.

rijeka’s refinery still isn’t operating at full capacity

For Croatia in particular, the Rijeka refinery is particularly important, but its operation was briefly disrupted on Friday by a lightning strike on a substation. Umičević believes that if the problem is only with the substation, the fault could be fixed relatively quickly, but stresses that this is a situation that should not be ignored. He added that the Rijeka refinery is in any case not yet operating at full capacity because certain tests are still expected to be completed, and it should reach full capacity next year. “Especially now, the Rijeka refinery is not operating at full capacity, because the completion of some tests is still expected. Only next year will Rijeka operate at full capacity. But what is important right now is that there is production, so we aren’t dependent on imports,” he noted.

diesel prices will probably increase again

Diesel prices could rise again from next week, Umičević believes. Although the oil price has fallen in the meantime, the diesel price has remained high and continues to rise. “I think prices will rise again next week, for a very simple reason – the diesel price is rising, as is the petrol price. What is absurd, or a paradox, is that oil prices have not risen as much as the diesel price in particular,” says Umičević. “At the beginning of the Iran-US conflict in the Strait of Hormuz the oil price was around 71 dollars per barrel, and at its highest it reached 126 dollars. The diesel price then rose from around 750 to 1,300 dollars. After the situation calmed down, oil fell to around 90, and today it is around 94 dollars, while the diesel price has remained practically the same and continues to rise,” he states.

He nevertheless expects that any price increase will not be large, but notes that the final decision also depends on the Government.

“there will be enough gas, but the price of it is another thing”

As for gas, Umičević believes that the goal of filling Croatia’s Okoli storage facility to 85 percent by the 1st of October is realistic. “A month or a month and a half ago we were at around 51 percent full. Croatia has enough gas and a relatively good mix of sources – we have the LNG terminal, domestic production (which is smaller, admittedly), and diversified other sources. I think it is realistic for Croatia to reach 85 percent,” says Umičević.

He added that one of the problems is that the gas price on the futures market is lower than the current one, so storage users do not find it profitable to buy gas now at higher prices. “The key problem is that future gas prices are lower than current ones. That’s why it doesn’t pay for storage users to buy now at high prices and later sell at lower ones. However, the Government has taken certain decisions, and HEP has been given the task of filling the storage to 85 percent,” he said.

He believes there is currently no reason for concern about gas quantities, but stresses that the question of price is something else. “There will be enough gas, just as there will be enough diesel, the only question is at what price it will be sold at. Gas prices have seriously fluctuated, and after the initial summer price increase the situation has stabilised somewhat. When everything is averaged out, there should not be a significant increase in the gas price either, especially because the state already subsidises the price,” he concluded.

World.title: Madise only candidate for Estonia's presidential election
World.content:
Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise was the only candidate officially registered for Estonia's presidential election during the registration process, which closed on Monday.

Seventy-five members of the 101-seat Riigikogu nominated Madise as a candidate on Monday morning. She has cross-party support from Reform, Eesti 200, the Social Democratic Party and Isamaa factions as well as unaffiliated MPs.

The deadline for nominations closed at 6 p.m. on Monday and candidates needed at least 21 signatures to be put forward.

Kadri Masing, media advisor to the Election Commission, told ERR on Monday evening that Madise was the only candidate nominated for the first round of the election.

On Tuesday at 3 p.m., the National Electoral Committee will meet to register her as a candidate.

Madise will need 68 votes to be elected president by the parliament. Reform Party faction chair Õnne Pillak said Madise has enough votes to win.

Ülle Madise Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"I believe that those who have already supported the candidate with their signatures will come and also cast their vote in support of her. I think there is also an expectation in society that we will elect Estonia's new president in the Riigikogu on September 2," she said.

Social Democratic Party chair Lauri Läänemets said Isamaa's support came as a surprise to him.

"The previous evening, before Isamaa's decision to support Ülle Madise, Isamaa MPs were still seeking signatures from unaffiliated MPs for Tiit Land. Clearly, in terms of their ratings, they found themselves in a situation where they were forced to make a U-turn," he said.

Two Isamaa MPs, deputy faction chair Priit Sibul and chair Helir Valdor Seeder, did not add their signatures to Madise's candidacy. However, faction member Lea Danilson-Järg said the party is not split over the subject.

"We reached a consensus decision that we support Ülle Madise's candidacy for president. I think it is simply a matter of who managed to get there to add their signature. There is no reason to think that there are some kind of political games going on here, because I don't think there are," she said.

Martin Helme and Mihhail Kõlvart, Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Of the parliamentary parties, EKRE and the Center Party did not support Madise's candidacy. EKRE chair Martin Helme said that he would continue Mart Helme's campaign and was prepared to nominate him in the Electoral College if the Riigikogu fails to elect a president.

Center Party chair Mihhail Kõlvart had previously expressed support for TalTech Rector Tiit Land.

"The Center Party's position has not changed. In our view, there should be an election, not an appointment. Since there will be no election in the Riigikogu, we have no desire to participate in an appointment," Kõlvart said.

World.title: Budget 2027: Reform wants to reduce deficit, Eesti 200 to support economy
World.content:
Negotiations for next year's budget start on Tuesday, and the coalition parties Reform and Eesti 200 want to prioritise cutting the deficit and supporting the economy.

Reform wants to cut the deficit by at least half a percentage point of GDP.

"At most, next year's budget deficit could be 4 percent. What makes achieving this goal easier is that our economy is growing – not vigorously, but still – people are working and taxes are coming in," said Annely Akkermann (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu Finance Committee.

Another favorable factor is the easing of inflation.

"Indexed expenditures, pension expenditures – those indices will be relatively small next year. If pensions are indexed to inflation and wage growth, then that index will be smaller next year. There also should not be very great pressure from wage costs, because the purchasing power of wages has been maintained," she said.

Annely Akkermann. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Coalition partner Eesti 200 wants to support the economy and people.

"We have earmarked 5 percent for defense spending well in advance, and we should increase the rest of the state budget so that we can maintain economic growth and improve competitiveness. We should not reverse investments; investments make up a large part of the budget. Estonia is a major investor, but I think we should continue with that," said Education Minister and Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas.

Kallas is demanding a pay rise for teachers, additional funding for vocational education and digital development.

"Reducing the budget deficit means the need to make cuts, and to cut education, healthcare and the social sector. At the moment, I do not see where those cuts should come from. We have slowed expenditure growth there quite significantly – by hundreds of millions. I do not see that we have any room to hold back there," she said.

As the coalition does not have enough votes to pass the budget by itself, it will need support from other parties or non-aligned MPs in the Riigikogu to do so.

Kristina Kallas. Source: Jürgen Randma/riigikantselei

Center Party MP Andrei Korobeinik says his party will not support a budget that does not improve the state of public finances.

"The main problem is the very large budget deficit, and the coalition has not proposed a single solution for how we will reduce it in the medium term, and there is a serious risk that before the elections there will be a desire to hand out money everywhere," he said.

If the budget is not adopted, the state will continue operating next year proportionally on the basis of this year's budget.

World.title: Estonian shooter wins world clay pigeon gold in sporting first
World.content:
Shooter Veikko Tihvan has made Estonian sports history by winning the FITASC Compak Sporting World Championships in Rio Salso, Italy.

Tihvan initially shared first place with multiple European and world championship medalist Charles Bardou of France after both hit 197 of 200 targets in Thursday's competition.

A shoot-off beckoned, which Tihvan won after beating the French competitor by one target, making him the first Estonian to win the title.

Clay pigeon shooting is a type of practical hunting shooting which simulates real-world hunting conditions, instead of having flat and static ranges. Not "pigeons" as such, the targets are saucer shaped, made of pulverized limestone and brightly colored.

Compak Sporting is a discipline of clay pigeon shooting governed internationally by FITASC (Fédération Internationale de Tir aux Armes Sportives de Chasse). As its name suggests, it is held on a compact shooting layout designed for use in a smaller area, compared with standard competitive clay pigeon shooting.

World.title: Nearly 1,900 basic school graduates still lack a school place as year begins
World.content:
A week before the start of the new school year, 1,893 basic school graduates in Estonia are without a school place; of them, 761 live in Tallinn, said Kadi Serbak, adviser at the Ministry of Education (HTM).

According to Serbak, HTM monitors the situation of finding school places daily. Since continued admissions to schools are still underway, HTM does not yet have a complete overview of young people who have not found a new study place after finishing basic school. Schools must enter admitted students into the Estonian Education Information System, from which HTM can see how many students are still without a school place.

HTM's project manager for compulsory education, Külli Solo, said that many schools do not do this during the admissions process, and there are young people who have received a school place but have not been entered into the information system.

The final number of basic school graduates who will not continue their studies will be known around 10 September. According to HTM data, in previous years about 800 basic school graduates have not continued their studies. The forecast is the same for this year.

Serbak said the ministry is trying to find solutions to the current situation in cooperation with local governments.

The ministry is analysing how to make basic school graduation and finding school places smoother and less stressful next year. "We have also informed the city of Tallinn that we would like to discuss options for increasing the number of preparatory study places ordered at Tallinn Applied College," Serbak said.

Continued admissions underway

Ülle Matsin, head of HTM's department of general and vocational education, told ERR last week that schools are conducting continued admissions every day, which means that eventually all students will find a study place.

"There is definitely a study place available to fulfil compulsory education, and if students currently still need counselling, they can confidently contact the schools where admissions are still ongoing," Matsin said.

"All learners will find opportunities to study. Through cooperation between the state and the city, study places in Tallinn should ultimately be available for all students," she confirmed.

Tallinn deputy mayor Andrei Kante said last week that the reason so many young people still lack clarity about their study options at the end of August is that basic school is being completed by young people without learning skills.

Matsin agreed that basic education holds several keys: a basic school graduate should receive guidance on where to continue studying and be aware that vocational fields offer many learning opportunities.

"We have actually pointed this out earlier in our messaging — that career counselling in basic school is important, and preparing the student at the end of the third school stage to move forward is crucial. In that respect, he is undoubtedly right," the ministry official said.

Tartu also has young people without school places

As of Friday, Tartu had around one hundred young people who have not found a school place, have not looked for one, or have left Estonia altogether, such as Ukrainian war refugees. This number is still constantly changing, said Riho Raave, head of Tartu's education department.

He said continued admissions are underway in some upper secondary schools and vocational institutions in Tartu, such as Tartu Applied College and Tartu Art School. "Applications are ongoing and the process is still underway, so I think by 1 September there will be even fewer who have not found a study place," Raave noted.

In connection with compulsory education, preparatory study will also begin for the first time this academic year. It is intended for young people up to age 18 who need support after basic school to move on to the next level of education.

According to Raave, the problem in Tartu is that all state‑funded preparatory study places at both Tartu Art School and the Applied College are already full.

Raave said schools had the option to admit students to preparatory study on their own. "Students applied, schools accepted them, but now there are no preparatory study places left for the most complex group of students — those who cannot find a school place," he explained. Raave believes more places need to be created.

Preparatory study should be an extreme measure

Solo said that ongoing continued admissions may still bring changes to preparatory study places, but negotiations with local governments are underway regarding the number of study places.

"Preparatory study is an extreme measure, intended specifically for those 800 young people who do not continue studying," Solo said.

In early August, it became clear that HTM wants to begin admissions to preparatory study next year starting from 1 September — that is, after basic and continued admissions. This should ensure that preparatory study is offered only to those young people who do not have a study place by 1 September or who need additional support.

World.title: Financial Intelligence Unit awaits restoration of powers by Riigikogu
World.content:
A bill aimed at clarifying the Financial Intelligence Unit's (FIU) access to banking data and restoring its ability to conduct on-site inspections has passed its first reading in the Riigikogu.

The final vote could come as early as October. Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise, now the only formally registered presidential candidate, has endorsed the bill and, if it passes and she is elected president, it could end up on her desk for assent or veto.

The bill would address two major restrictions on the FIU: its ability to access bank account information through the enforcement register and its ability to carry out on-site inspections at banks and other institutions.

The legislation follows concerns raised by Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise about the legal basis for government agencies accessing bank account information through the enforcement register. The unit's access was suspended by Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200).

The restrictions also affected the Tax and Customs Board (MTA), which was unable to request certain data through the register for tax-fraud prevention and other duties until the government reversed course in May.

The government has since proposed amendments specifying when and how the FIU and MTA may request banking data through the enforcement register. The Finance Ministry has stressed that the amendments do not create new substantive powers to access banking secrecy, but clarify that existing powers may be exercised through the enforcement register, a secure and logged channel.

Under the proposed framework, requests would have to be justified and logged, while people would have the ability to challenge an administrative act authorising access.

The Estonian-founded LHV Pank, for example, has stopped providing bank account statements to the FIU, saying the unit has no legal right to request them. The Tallinn Administrative Court ruled in the bank's favor, although the FIU has appealed.

FIU chief Matis Mäeker said the restrictions are also affecting Estonia's ability to cooperate with its international partners, and that this is harming Estonia in return.

In her role as Chancellor of Justice, Ülle Madise raised concerns which led to a diminishing of the FIU's powers. However, a bill restoring them could end up being signed by her if it passes and if she gets elected president in early September. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"If you are a good partner, you get answers more quickly; if you are a worse partner, you get answers more slowly. At the moment, we are in a situation where we cannot answer all questions as we do not have the right to request this data," Mäeker said.

Mäeker gave as an example one case in which fraudulently obtained money was transferred to another country one day, then by the following day had already been moved to accounts at 14 different credit institutions, making recovering the funds increasingly difficult.

The FIU's powers were further restricted by a Supreme Court ruling in January. The body can no longer physically visit, for example, a bank or a gambling company, in order to check compliance with its anti-money-laundering (AML) procedures.

On-site inspections are an "irreplaceable" tool for a supervisory authority, Mäeker added.

"One thing is what happens on paper, another is what happens in real life. To understand whether what is on paper actually corresponds to reality, you can only find out on site," he said.

The bill would address both issues. It would clarify the division and extent of the powers of the FIU and MTA to obtain information needed for their duties, particularly bank account and account data, while also restoring the FIU's ability to conduct on-site inspections.

The opposition parties have signaled support for the bill, though some MPs have questioned its lengthy notification deadlines. Aivar Kokk (Isamaa), a member of the Riigikogu Finance Committee, said he could not understand how it could ever be justified to keep a person unaware for so long that their bank account had been examined. Andrei Korobeinik (Center) warned that notification could potentially be postponed repeatedly.

Under the terms of the bill, a person or company would normally be notified five years after their bank account statement was obtained. In certain circumstances, notification could be postponed for up to another five years — meaning that in some cases, the person or company might not learn about the examination for as long as 10 years.

Maris Lauri (Reform), who is leading work on the bill in the Finance Committee, said she wants to hear further justification from interest groups regarding the time limits. She noted that the current deadlines may be optimal, but discussions are continuing. If consideration proceeds without major obstacles, the Riigikogu could adopt the bill as early as October.

FIU chief Matis Mäeker. Source: ERR

LHV has raised broader privacy and legal concerns about the proposed rules. Ants Soone, LHV's head of compliance, wrote that since 2021 the FIU has no longer been an investigative body and lacks the right to conduct surveillance measures. He argued that treating the examination of bank statements as a surveillance measure could raise questions about whether evidence obtained in this way would be admissible in court.

Soone also objected to the possibility of retaining information covered by bank confidentiality for five to 10 years "just in case," arguing that mass retention of personal data like this could conflict with EU fundamental-rights law.

Madise has also weighed in, saying she did not oppose the bill in principle. She agreed that the FIU and/or the MTA should be able to access bank account statements via the enforcement register when investigating specific suspicions, but said the Riigikogu should carefully consider whether the proposed notification periods are truly necessary or should be shortened.

If the bill passes, it would address concerns Madise raised as Chancellor of Justice. Madise is, at the time of writing, the only formally registered candidate in the presidential elections taking place in the Riigikogu, with a few hours to go until registration closes. If the 74 MPs who signed in favour of her candidacy — or a minimum of 68 MPs — translate that backing into a vote for Madise as president on September 2-3, she will become the next head of state.

If that happened, she would then have the power as president to sign or veto legislation on the same topic herself.

The money laundering bill's final reading may take place in October, as things stand.

World.title: Kaamos art grant to focus on artists over 60
World.content:
The Kaamos art scholarship, awarded for the first time last year, is this year intended for artists over 60. The amount of the scholarship is 25,000 euros.

While the focus in the first year was on women artists, Kaamos has now decided that the scholarship's target group will change each year in order to draw attention to different groups within the Estonian art field and their work, and to keep the scholarship diverse and evolving over time.

The Kaamos art scholarship was established by the Estonian Centre for Contemporary Art and Estonian-owned investment firm Kaamos Group. Candidates are invited to apply until 28 September; artists may apply themselves or be nominated by someone working in the art field or by an art institution.

The recipient will be chosen by a jury consisting of Kumu curator Eha Komissarov, head of Tartu Art House and chair of the Tartu Artists' Union Peeter Talvistu, artist and artist‑salary recipient Marge Monko, one representative of the CCA and two representatives of Kaamos Group. The composition of the jury rotates partially every two years.

Last year, the first Kaamos scholarship was awarded to Anna Mari Liivrand. "The Kaamos scholarship came unexpectedly and at a very right moment for me," said last year's laureate. "With the support of the scholarship, I have been able to fully dedicate myself to both larger and smaller exhibition projects, and I see that it has helped me create more substantial and exciting works."

World.title: Government to begin next year's budget talks on Tuesday
World.content:
The government will begin discussions on next year's budget and the state budget strategy at Stenbock House on Tuesday.

Deputy director of government communications Liis Velsker said that on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, members of the government will start discussions on next year's state budget and the state budget strategy for the next four years.

On Thursday, the Ministry of Finance will present the summer economic forecast to the cabinet.

The economic forecast is used by the government and parliament when making budget‑policy decisions, and by businesses when preparing strategic plans. The explanatory memorandum also gives the wider public an overview of recent economic developments and the outlook for the next four years.

"Over the coming weeks, the government will discuss the budget. At the end of September, the government will approve the revenue, expenditure and other measures of the state budget and the state budget strategy, as well as the Health Insurance Fund's budget position for the next four years, and all draft laws related to next year's state budget. The goal is also to approve the allocation of EU support for the 2028–2034 period — the state plan," Velsker said.

She added that at the end of September, the government must submit the draft state budget for 2027 to the Riigikogu and approve the state budget strategy for 2027–2030. Before that, the government will hear the opinion of the Fiscal Council.

World.title: Iraq, Qatar provide oil for loading inside Hormuz via bids
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Trade sources reported on Monday that Iraq’s national oil marketer, SOMO, and QatarEnergy are presenting crude oil through unusual bids that mandate purchasers to load cargoes within the Strait of Hormuz.

SOMO announced that it is offering Basrah Medium and Basrah Heavy crude for loading in September from either the Basrah oil port or a single point mooring, along with the necessary supporting facilities, as reported by Reuters.

QatarEnergy provided free-on-board oil loading at al-Shaheen, Qatar Marine, and Qatar Land ports in September and October.

Earlier, SOMO provided substantial discounts on Basrah crude in August to entice customers to load shipments from the Strait of Hormuz.

SOMO asked potential term purchasers to designate contractual volumes of Basrah Medium or Basrah Heavy crude for complimentary onboard delivery from the Basrah Oil Terminal or other port-related infrastructure.

Iraq’s oil marketer provided discounts ranging between $25 and $27 per barrel on Basrah Medium, according to the loading period. It provided discounts of $27.80 to $29.80 a barrel for Basrah Heavy.

Maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz decreased due to ongoing military operations in the region and heightened shipping security risks.

The significant price reduction aims to compensate for rising maritime insurance costs and freight expenses by transferring transit risk to purchasers.

World.title: Iraq to introduce new banknotes with three zeros removed
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq intends to remove three zeros from its currency to modernize financial transactions, reduce physical cash circulation, and return stockpiled funds to the official banking system.

Under the suggestion, a 25,000-Iraqi dinar note would become 25 Iraqi dinars, but the currency’s purchasing power and true financial value would stay unaffected.

According to Jamal Kocher, a Kurdish member of the Iraqi parliament’s finance committee, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has asked for the removal of zeros from invoices.

Kocher told The New Region that if the plan is implemented, 1,000 Iraqi dinars would be converted to one dinar, while 25,000 dinars would be equivalent to 25 dinars.

Earlier in August, Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad acknowledged the plan to eliminate the zeros and modify the currency.

The redenomination strategy aims to bring undeclared cash, estimated to be between 8 and 10 trillion Iraqi dinars that are currently held outside banks, back into official channels. This initiative seeks to combat crime, corruption, and money laundering.

According to the idea, everyday prices, incomes, and savings will alter correspondingly, resulting in a direct mathematical shift rather than a change in actual wealth.

Iraq has sought printing partners in the United Kingdom and Australia, as well as its traditional suppliers in France and Germany, to create an estimated 7.5 billion new banknotes.

While government officials such as the Communications Minister and Finance Committee members have emphasized the importance of an official implementation date, the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) has yet to present a formal draft bill to parliament.

World.title: Iraq to raise oil exports via Turkey’s Ceyhan to 750,000 bpd
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Oil announced on Sunday a proposal to increase oil exports through the Turkish port of Ceyhan to 750,000 barrels per day by using tanker trucks to transport crude oil from southern oilfields.

The spokesperson for the Iraqi Oil Ministry, Salim al-Rikabi, told the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA) that the plan includes increasing exports through southern ports.

Iraq and Turkey recently inked a one-year short-term deal to continue operations through the critical Iraq-Turkey oil pipeline.

The agreement, reached in Ankara following discussions between Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar and Iraqi Oil Minister Basim Khudair, guarantees the ongoing transportation of at least 750,000 barrels of Iraqi crude oil per day to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.

Turkey’s state-owned crude oil and natural gas pipeline corporation (BOTAS) signed an agreement with Iraq’s State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) and the North Oil Company (NOC).

The new deal is now valid for 12 months until both countries develop a new, long-term legislative framework.

The previous agreement, which was reached in 1973, officially expired on July 27.

The short extension of the deal is crucial for Iraq’s revenue from oil exports, as Baghdad seeks alternative export routes to mitigate risks linked to the Strait of Hormuz.

World.title: Eto’o urges support for embattled FIFA president Infantino
World.content:
Paris – Former Cameroon star Samuel Eto’o has thrown his support behind beleaguered FIFA president Gianni Infantino, saying he “hasn’t done anything wrong” despite facing mounting pressure to step down over a controversial World Cup sell-off plan.

Infantino has come under intense scrutiny since the collapse of a proposal to secure private investment in FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup.

UEFA, which oversees European football, has threatened a boycott of FIFA competitions with several continental and national federations also withdrawing their support for Infantino.

However, Eto’o, president of the Cameroonian football federation, dismissed criticism of Infantino’s leadership, suggesting the backlash was driven largely by political manoeuvring ahead of FIFA’s presidential election next year.

“I don’t think that President Gianni Infantino has done anything wrong,” the former Barcelona, Inter Milan and Chelsea striker told CNN.

“I think the timing of all of that is because there’s an election coming out.”

Infantino’s plan, which would reportedly have distributed substantial funding to FIFA’s 211 member associations, faced strong opposition from several confederations and was ultimately abandoned.

The FIFA president remains under pressure, with the possibility of a no-confidence vote being triggered. UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and CONCACAF — which governs North and Central America and the Caribbean — have all voiced concerns over FIFA’s direction in recent weeks.

But the Confederation of African Football (CAF) earlier this month “unanimously reconfirmed its support” for Infantino, and Eto’o’s backing is aligned with that position.

“President Gianni Infantino has changed football,” said Eto’o, urging fellow African countries to support the Swiss official.

“He’s given opportunities to nations that didn’t have those opportunities to take part in the most beautiful tournament, the World Cup. He enabled smaller nations to get seats at these competitions.

“He has helped our continent. He’s helped our federations to develop much more quickly, and we need to acknowledge that. We need to accept and recognise what he’s done, and we should support him for everything he’s done up to now.”

World.title: Trump claims Iran ‘collapsing’ as US threatens ‘economic D-Day’
World.content:
Washington – US President Donald Trump said Monday that Iran was “collapsing” as Washington prepared to announce the details of a new economic pressure campaign that Tehran has derided as an admission of defeat.

Almost six months into their war, the two sides are locked in a stalemate, with peace talks stalled, Iran keeping the key Strait of Hormuz shut and Washington persisting with a naval counter-blockade of Iran.

Under political pressure at home over the economic impacts of the conflict, Trump has pivoted away from military action to economic levers.

“IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!” the president posted Monday in his trademark all-caps style on his social media platform Truth Social.

His remarks came hours after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, in a column for the Financial Times, declared that an “economic D-Day” had begun against Tehran and warned that any country that continued to enable the Islamic republic would become a “global pariah”.

Bessent also claimed on X that the US had “dismantled Iran’s military capabilities, destroyed nearly 100 percent of its military factories, and buried its nuclear programme”.

Iran responded with defiance, saying the latest US measures were an admission of military defeat, and it warned countries against aiding Washington.

Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi posted on X that the US turn to financial warfare proved Bessent’s claims false.

“Your narrative doesn’t add up,” Gharibabadi said, asking why, if Washington had achieved its goals, “there is a need for ‘the largest financial invasion in history’ and the mobilisation of ‘all institutions and powers’ of the United States!

“Is this a victory or an admission of America’s defeat?”

The US and Israel linked the launch of their war in February to Iran’s nuclear programme, but the focus since the early days of fighting has been on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global oil and gas supplies.

Tehran continues to blockade the strait, which it did not restrict before the war, driving up global inflation and heaping domestic pressure on Trump ahead of mid-term elections in November.

– Oil exports plunge –

Bessent was due to set out details of the US plan on Monday, but it is unclear how much more economic pressure Washington can put on Tehran.

The US naval blockade of Iran has seen its oil exports via the Strait of Hormuz fall from two million barrels a day pre-war to just 0.4 million by mid-August, according to maritime tracker Kpler.

Meanwhile, the country has been under crushing international sanctions for decades, with a brief period of easing under a 2015 nuclear deal that Trump later ripped up as part of a “maximum pressure” campaign.

The Islamic republic has weathered those efforts and, before the war, continued to export millions of barrels of oil, mostly to China, and evade sanctions through complex international financial networks.

Bessent and Trump have both warned countries against helping Iran, signalling a shift in their focus, with the Treasury secretary’s FT column dwelling on nations who “appease” and “enable” Iran.

Tehran responded on Monday by warning countries not to cooperate with the US efforts. Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said taking part would “definitely have its own consequences”.

For ordinary Iranians, the standoff is likely to bring only more economic pain after years of rampant inflation, which in December and January fuelled massive anti-government protests.

Sarah Hassanbeigi, a 32-year-old pharmacist in Tehran, put it simply: “It’s really very difficult. I don’t think people can really take this much longer.”

On Sunday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian admitted that Iran faced “many problems in society”.

“We are striving with all our hearts to overcome inflation, livelihood problems, unemployment, and to secure the future of the people, so that they can live with dignity and pride,” Pezeshkian said.

– Delegation from Pakistan –

Last week, the Iranian president, considered a relative moderate, said Tehran should “bring the war to an end now as we are in a position of power and dignity”.

That followed supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei appointing hardliners to key security positions.

Hassanbeigi said she wanted peace. “Naturally, negotiations mean that both sides have to compromise. My personal opinion is that Iran should compromise now,” she told AFP.

Throughout the war, diplomatic efforts, pushed on by mediators, have sought a negotiated end to the conflict.

On Monday, Pakistan’s army chief was expected in Iran. Islamabad was a leading mediator in talks that helped secure an April ceasefire that later fell apart.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi was also due in Iran on Tuesday, as Muscat and Tehran seek a deal on regulating passage through Hormuz.

World.title: Liverpool must improve on ‘unacceptable’ season, says Van Dijk
World.content:
Liverpool – Virgil van Dijk said Liverpool “need to show a reaction” from a bitterly disappointing season that cost Arne Slot his job as manager, but called for patience with new boss Andoni Iraola.

The Reds needed a 99th-minute equaliser from the penalty spot by Dominik Szoboszlai to rescue a 2-2 draw at Newcastle on the opening weekend of the Premier League season.

Slot guided Liverpool to glory and a 20th league title in his debut campaign in 2024/25, but paid the price for finishing fifth last season when he was dismissed in May.

Many of the same flaws were in evidence in Iraola’s first outing at St James’ Park as Newcastle sliced open the Liverpool defence on the counter-attack.

But they twice came from behind to avoid a losing start to the new season.

“It’s absolutely normal in any type of profession, work, whatever you do, if you come in new and you have new plans and new ideas, then it takes a bit of time with new players,” said Van Dijk.

“It’s down to us to do it as soon as we can, as soon as possible, because we want to improve, we want to win, we want to be better. That’s what we are going to try to do.

“We need to show a reaction from last year, that we are much better than last year, because this was very unacceptable.”

Iraola has not been aided by a lack of new arrivals in the transfer market.

Despite the departure of club legend Mohamed Salah and a long-term injury to Hugo Ekitike, Liverpool have only added Spanish winger Victor Munoz in attacking areas as well as defenders Jeremy Jacquet and Ronald Araujo.

Paris Saint-Germain’s two-time Champions League winner Bradley Barcola has been linked with a move to Anfield, while two bids for Brighton winger Yankuba Minteh have reportedly been turned down.

“Everyone wants to see quality arrive regardless and I fully trust the club and the board to make the right decisions,” Van Dijk added.

“That’s the only thing I can say, so let’s see what we are going to do.”

World.title: Iraq suggests a security council involving Iran, Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has officially suggested forming a joint security coordination council with Iran and Saudi Arabia to address what it calls a severe crisis of trust between the two regional powers.

The Security Affairs Adviser to the Prime Minister of Iraq, Qasim al-Araji, put forward the diplomatic initiative on behalf of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government to stabilize the region where Iraq strives to manage its own turbulent security climate.

Baghdad clearly planned the initiative to reconcile serious tensions between Riyadh and Tehran.

Tensions rose as Saudi Arabia intercepted multiple drones aimed at its oil facilities and capital. Riyadh denounced Iran-backed militias that operate from inside Iraq.

The idea comes during a very unstable period, including recent US-Saudi joint airstrikes targeting Popular Mobilization Forces’ (PMF) sites in Iraq and leading to serious criticism from Baghdad for sovereignty violations.

Baghdad is also pressuring Tehran for waivers for oil tankers from Iran’s navigation restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz.

Additionally, al-Araji underlined Iraq’s transition to ultimate domestic sovereignty.

With the scheduled withdrawal of the US-led international coalition forces from Iraq, Baghdad is adopting a strategy to put all armed factions and weaponry under strict state supervision, consolidating the country’s ultimate authority over war and peace choices.

Neither Saudi Arabia nor Iran has released a formal public response to the Iraqi initiative.

World.title: Iraq foreign reserves decline 11.6% to $86.17B in June 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Official financial statements from the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) show that Iraq’s foreign exchange reserves declined to $86.175 billion at the end of June 2026, marking a decrease of $11.257 billion (-11.6%) compared to the $97.432 billion recorded at the close of 2025.

According to reserve records published on Monday, August 24, 2026, the contraction followed an early-year peak above $102 billion before downward momentum set in through the second quarter.

Monthly Reserve Trajectory (H1 2026)

End of 2025 Baseline: $97.432 billion

January 2026: $101.082 billion

February 2026 (Peak): $102.131 billion

March 2026: $100.341 billion

April 2026: $97.809 billion

May 2026: $93.673 billion

June 2026:$86.175 billion(Month-over-month drop of $7.498 billion)

The overall drop reduced the local currency value of the total portfolio from 126.661 trillion IQD at the end of 2025 to 112.027 trillion IQD by June 30, 2026—a net decline of 14.634 trillion IQD (-11.6%).

Reserve Component End of 2025 (IQD) End of June 2026 (IQD) Net Change Change (%) Investments & Securities 93.266 Trillion 81.998 Trillion -11.268 Trillion -12.1% Monetary Gold Reserves 31.488 Trillion 29.415 Trillion -2.073 Trillion -6.6% Cash Vault Holdings 1.907 Trillion 0.614 Trillion -1.293 Trillion -67.8% Total Equivalent Value 126.661 Trillion 112.027 Trillion -14.634 Trillion -11.6%

The reserve reduction aligns with broader fiscal pressures in the first half of 2026, during which lower oil revenues widened the state budget deficit and prompted the central bank to meet elevated domestic foreign currency demand.

While liquid investment instruments fell by 11.268 trillion IQD to absorb trade financing and foreign wire settlements, cash assets held in central bank vaults rebounded moderately in June (up to 614 billion IQD from 366 billion IQD in May), even as overall foreign exchange reserves adjusted downward to $86.175 billion.

World.title: Assam: CM Himanta meets Nitin Gadkari, seeks flood-resilient highways, restoration of damaged roads
World.content:
Himata Biswa Sarma met Union Minister

on Monday in New Delhi. They had a discussion about the restoration of flood damaged National Highways and plans for enhancing the resilience of the state's highway network against the floods.

As per the official release, the meeting mainly focused on the immediate restoration of flood damaged National Highways as well as the long term important measures that should be taken to strengthen the infrastructure. This will help to improve the connectivity. The CM also emphasised the need for the evidence based planning to design the bridges to improve the drainage issue so that it can minimise the impact of floods and make the road connectivity smooth.

"Our discussions focused on restoring flood-damaged National Highways at the earliest and building more flood-resilient highways, using evidence-based planning to improve the design and placement of culverts and bridges," the Chief Minister said in a post on X following the meeting.
