World.title: ‘Grain’ revolution: How lost varieties of rice are coming back
World.content:
Biryani made with Kaima instead of Basmati, payesh made with Badshahbhog, risotto made with Assamâs Bora. With heirloom rice vanishing from Indian kitchens faster than they could be documented, this seemed, until not very long ago, nothing more than nostalgia.

The Green Revolutionâs push for high-yield monoculture had, over the years, pushed out many old types of rice. But now, several of those varieties, thought long gone, are staging a comeback â thanks to the efforts of farmers, conservationists, NGOs, restaurateurs, and a bit of help from some state govts.

Guardians of the grain

In coastal Karnatakaâs Nettanige village, Padma Shri awardee Sathyanarayana Beleri â everyone calls him âSeeding Sathyaâ â nurtures more than 100 traditional paddy varieties in grow bags outside his house.

Itâs a small selection from his vast collection of over 650 seed varieties, collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.

He has strains of flood-resistant Edekunhi and Nereguli, the medicinal Dodda Byra Nellu, and Kalanamak (also called âBuddha Riceâ). Heâs distributed seeds to hundreds of farmers across Karnataka and Kerala, as well as to agricultural universities nationwide. âRiceâ, he says, âcan be cultivated in grow bags, just like vegetables at home.





As climate change reshapes agriculture, conserving traditional, climate-resilient varieties is no longer a choice.

It is a necessity.â

Sathyanarayana Beleri with some of the more than 650 seed varieties he has collected from across India, Sri Lanka, Japan and the Philippines.

Further inland, entire families have turned conservation into a generational commitment. In Belthangady taluk, the Rao family has conserved 180-190 traditional varieties on 5.5 acres since B K Deva Rao started a seed bank in 1988. His son, Parameshwar Rao, points to a benefit beyond biodiversity.

âPaddy cultivation is among the best forms of groundwater recharge and rainwater harvesting,â he says. âStrong field bunds can retain water for nearly a week.

Even two cropping cycles can substantially improve the groundwater table.â Their prized variety, Kayame â a red rice â âhas a flavour rarely found in modern commercial varieties,â he adds.

Some 1,300km away in Chhattisgarh, Khemlal Dewangan, a maths teacher in Rajnandgaon district, started farming traditional paddy around 15 years ago.

Dewangan started with a handful of desi strains. He now has a collection of around 70 varieties.

His seed collection has grown through a nationwide network of farmers â brought together on WhatsApp â who test small quantities in their fields. âI now receive 10-15 enquiries a day from social media and word of mouth,â he says.

For him, the appeal goes beyond the market: he says traditional varieties are healthier, as they take longer to mature, absorbing more soil nutrients.

Roots of a revival

None of this happened by accident. Back in 2004, the UNâs second International Year of Rice, Kerala-based NGO Thanal decided something had to be done about Indiaâs vanishing rice varieties. They launched the Save Our Rice campaign through a workshop in Kumbalangi village. Thanal teamed up with Tamil Naduâs CREATE (a non-profit organisation) to run it, and the campaign took root in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Bengal, later spreading into Chhattisgarh.

Members of CREATE educate farmers about heirloom rice varieties on a farm in Tamil Nadu.

India had over one lakh varieties of rice in 1966, but by the time the campaign started, that number had dropped to around 30,000 â most locked away in university seed banks, rather than growing in farmersâ fields. The campaign has had a big impact on southern states. âIn the last 15-16 years, there has been a revival of traditional seeds in these states,â says Jayakumar C, executive director at Thanal. âToday, there are more than 25 or 30 farmers or groups doing traditional seeds in different parts of Kerala.

Thanalâs own centre in Wayanad now holds around 320- 330 varieties of rice.â

That demand has started showing up in the market. Thanal runs a regular shop now in Thiruvananthapuram. Jayakumar says Kaima (also called Jeerakasala or Jeeraga Samba), a traditional variety, has become popular for biryani. Brands have caught on, too. Thondi, from a Wayanad farmer-producer company, sells online and via courier across Keralaâs cities, even as Mappila Chamba has built a following.

âTraditional rice tends to be more filling,â says Jayakumar. You feel full after eating less, unlike white rice hybrids. Also, the longer shelf life and taste after cooking is winning over urban households, especially the older people.â

When state stepped in

In Tamil Nadu, govt push gave the revival momentum. According to Suresh Kanna, project director at CREATE Trust, state govt began promoting six native varieties some 10 years ago under the State Heritage Rice Mission: Mappillai Samba, Karuppu Kavuni, Thooyamalli, Poongar, Kaattuyaanam and Kichili Samba.

âToday, they are liked by consumers and can be seen in organic shops across the state. They also fetch good income for the farmers.

A Kavuni farmer can get up to Rs 200 for a kilo. My calculation is that more than one lakh farmers in the state are now cultivating traditional paddy varieties,â Kanna says.

Even in Karnataka, grassroots efforts are now finding institutional backing. KVK Dakshina Kannada has begun field trials of 10 traditional varieties sourced from Beleri, aiming to identify strains suited to the coastal region, and reintroduce them into local food systems.

Karnatakaâs agriculture department has documented 2,164 traditional landraces (local, traditional varieties that evolved through natural and human selection to adapt to a specific geographic and climatic environment) across 20 crops, with paddy topping the list at 1,469 varieties, under its Conservation and Promotion of Landraces Programme.

Rs 1.3 crore in incentives went to 490 farmers in 2025-26 for viable seed samples.

The effort centres on custodian farmers who âcontinued cultivating them on small patches of land,â as department director GT Puthra puts it.

The department is now supporting GI registration for varieties including Kagga paddy, Rajmudi paddy, Bijapur Jola, Joni Bella and Kumbi Mudli, and plans incentives for 15 âforgotten treasureâ shops.

Farm to fork, fork to fame

A few restaurants are actively championing rare, indigenous rice over commercial varieties.

Edible Archives in Goa works with regional grains like Thavala Kannan from Wayanad (a red rice from Palakkad, whose name means âfrogâs eyesâ in Malayalam), and Pokkali, which brings a distinct coastal terroir.

The Kolkata-based Amar Khamar, both a heritage-grain retail brand and restaurant, is entirely built around Bengalâs native rice. Its signature is âChhuti-r Bhatâ, an 11-course meal following the traditional sequence of a Bengali meal, centred on heirloom varieties like Sugondhi Chine Kamini Aatap.

âChhuti-r Bhatâ in Kolkataâs Amar Khamar, which is an 11-course meal centred on heirloom rice varieties.

That influence has spread to other restaurants in the city. Sienna Cafe sources Chine Kamini, Radha Tilok, Kanakchur and Tulaipanji Atop from Amar Khamar; Yokocho, a Japanese alleyway-inspired bar and BBQ, draws on Kanakchur, Tulaipanji Atop and Karpurkanti; Red Bari incorporates Shatia, Mallifulo and Khejur Chhari.

Juhi Punwani, head of kitchen operations at Amar Khamar, has built a career around collecting the many myths and stories behind Bengalâs native rice varieties.

âGobindobhog is not the only heritage rice in Bengal,â she says. A rice called Radhuni Pagol literally means âthe cook gone crazyâ, after lore that its fragrance once filled a kitchen so completely that the cook couldnât think of anything else.

Tulaipanji of North Bengal gets its name from how the cooked rice turns light and airy like cotton (tula); Khejur Chhari is named for the date palm its grains resemble; Radha Tilokâs dark-tipped grain evokes Radhaâs tilak mark.

âEvery rice here has a beautiful story and a journey, and thatâs what weâre trying to showcase,â says Punwani, whose team has worked to bring back over 100 varieties, keeping around 50 in active rotation.

A look at select traditional rice varieties and the regions they are associated with across India.

This past summer, that ambition crossed continents, as Amar Khamar toured France and Germany. In Paris, working with sommelier Rajat Parr, the team built an 80-guest, 10-course tasting menu entirely around rice.

Kanakchur turned up as fritters with brown butter hollandaise, Sundarbansgrown Karpurkanti and Chine Kamini appeared as aatapan alongside a jackfruit-seed mung dal, Barddhamanâs Mohansal was served boiled, the meal closing with a Jhargram Fine Black Rice phirni.

In Stuttgart, the team built a fully vegan Bengali tasting menu, rice carrying the meal from a humble jhal muri to a coconut-milk Badshahbhog payesh for dessert.

A separate 200-guest winery event tested whether the format could scale â from Karpurkanti-paired lentils, a Chine Kamini peas pulao to Sunday lamb curry and Badshahbhog milk-rice. âNone of this would be possible without the relationships we have built with a network of farmers,â says Punwani, who executed the menu in Europe.

The traceability problem

But as heritage rice travels from the farm into retail shelves, a different problem emerges: knowing whether whatâs being sold is really what it claims to be.

One store has built its entire business around solving exactly that. In Chennaiâs Mylapore sits a store unlike any other. Spirit of the Earth calls itself a âretail store and experience centreâ, where customers come to see, touch, feel and know the story of every rice.

Opened in 2017, itâs the retail face of a project that Sheela Balaji, chairperson of NGO AIM For Seva, began over a decade ago, built on a principle she believes the heritage-rice surge often misses: traceability.

âUnfortunately, certain grains are being sold as certain varieties, which is inaccurate,â says Balaji.

âThe minute you say heritage rice, people will just come and buy it. But who is taking accountability? How do you know if itâs really diabetic friendly? So, I started this project more than a decade ago, first and foremost by building a seed bank. All the rice that you see in our store is grown from our farm in Manjakkudi, a village in Tiruvarur.â

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The 40-acre operation has grown as neighbouring farmers joined in, alongside a seed bank built from years of Balajiâs fieldwork with growers in Manipur, Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh.

For Balaji, the mission is beyond nutrition or nostalgia. âRice in our culture is Lakshmi,â she says. âAnd reintroducing its forgotten names and forms, one customer at a time, is as much about restoring that reverence as it is about the grain itself.â

World.title: 'Dog-barking' remark on students: Tejashwi says BPSC official 'mirrors CM's language'; demands removal
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Bihar leader of opposition and

leader

has demanded an apology from BPSC examination controller Rajesh Kumar over his "dog-barking" remark against protesting students.

While RJD scion also took a sharp dig at chief minister Samrat Choudhary, alleging official's language "mirrors the CM's language.

"

Tejashwi said immediate action should be taken against the official, warning that such comments could set a wrong precedent in Bihar and encourage officials to speak disrespectfully to students and the public.

Speaking to news agency ANI, Tejashwi criticised the Bihar government over the ongoing protests linked to the 70th BPSC examination.

He said the examination controllerâs remarks reflected the âlanguage of the chief ministerâ.

âThis official should be removed immediately and made to apologise,â Tejashwi said. He alleged that students and young people were being ignored and that repeated exam-related controversies had not led to anyone being held accountable.

Tejashwi also accused the government of failing to fix responsibility for repeated cancellations, alleged paper leaks and irregularities in competitive examinations.





'Elephant walks, dogs bark'

The row began after BPSC Examination Controller Rajesh Kumar was asked about allegations of irregularities and paper leaks.

Responding to questions, Kumar reportedly said: âHaathi chale bazaar, kutta bhaunke hazaarâ - meaning, âAn elephant walks through the market while a thousand dogs bark.â

Their protest has also focused on the proposed Teacher Recruitment Examination-4 (TRE-4). Students are opposing the plan to hold the examination in two phases across Bihar and are demanding that the official TRE-4 notification be released.

SC flags private access to sensitive PF, I-T data, asks Centre to prevent misuse by firms

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday expressed concern about a commercial technological ecosystem which allegedly accesses, retrieves and verifies sensitive individual information on provident fund and income tax returns and told the Centre about the desirability of devising an antidote to the problem with the assistance of domain experts.Hearing a PIL by Piyush Sharma, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana noted the matter essentially fell within policy domain but termed private access to sovereign data - individual information given to govt under legislative mandate - and its commercial exploitation as worrisome.Petitioner said his personal inquiry into the issue had revealed that "upon merely furnishing PAN and UAN details to a private verification workflow, the petitioner received complete employment history corresponding the said identifiers. World.title: Mizoram's 'misogynistic' marriage, divorce law faces challenge in SC
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Entrepreneur and Congress functionary Meriam L Hrangchal Monday challenged the constitutional validity of Mizo Marriage, Divorce and Inheritance of Property Act, 2014, which was enacted by Congress govt headed by Lal Thanhawla, terming it "misogynistic and pro-Mizo men".

Hrangchal, daughter of former deputy CM Lalhmingthanga, told a bench headed by CJI Surya Kant that the law, which codified customary law, applied to any person belonging to a Mizo tribe and extended to marriages where the male member belonged to a Mizo tribe.

The 2014 Act denies Mizo women, who marry outside the Mizo community, access to a comprehensive community-specific statutory framework governing marriage, property and inheritance, thereby infringing their right to equality, dignity and personal liberty under Articles 14 and 21, she said.

The law marginalises the independent identity of Mizo women and refuses them the benefits under the 2014 Act which extends to marriage between a Mizo man and a non-Mizo woman but does not cover marriage between a Mizo woman and a non-Mizo man, she said, citing her own marital relationship.

"The effect of such provisions is that Mizo women who marry non-Mizo men, and the children born out of such marriages, are excluded from the statutory regime, notwithstanding their subsisting connection to the Mizo community," she said.





The bench said the issue raised in her petition was important but asked why she was bypassing the high court. Her counsel said the community being small, she feared for her safety if her petition was heard by the Aizawl bench of Gauhati HC.

World.title: 22 million hectares of degraded land restored during 2011 and 2020
World.content:
NEW DELHI: India has restored nearly 22 million hectares of degraded and deforested land during the 2011-20 period as against its target of restoring 26 million hectares by 2030, said Union minister

at a UN conference Monday.

While addressing the 17th session (COP17) of the UNCCD conference in Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, he also pitched for "diversified, adequate, predictable and sustained international finance" for land restoration and drought resilience, saying it is not a cost, but an investment in food, water, biodiversity, livelihood and long-term resilience.

Underlining how the country's restoration efforts had generated approximately 1.2 billion person-days of employment during the 2011-20 period, he said these figures demonstrated restoration could deliver both environmental and socio-economic outcomes by reviving degraded landscapes while creating employment and supporting rural livelihoods.

According to Indiaâs second progress report on its land restoration efforts, covering the period 2011â2020, Telangana restored the maximum (4.2 million hectares) degraded area followed by Madhya Pradesh (3.8 million ha), Odisha (2.6 million ha), Gujarat (1.7 million ha) and Andhra Pradesh (1.6 million ha) through afforestation, water resource management, sustainable farming practices, agroforestry, mangrove restoration and natural regeneration of formerly forested land.





Indiaâs Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas shows that 97.8 million ha of land, or nearly 29.8% of the countryâs geographical area, are affected by land degradation and desertification. Around 82% of Indiaâs degraded land falls in nine states/UT - Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Jammu & Kashmir, Karnataka, Jharkhand, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana.

World.content:
NEW DELHI:

Monday said it would pass order on former Tehelka editor

The matter was heard by a single judge, Justice Alok Aradhe. Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state govt, contended that existence of the appeal was dependent on Tejpal either filing a certificate that he has surrendered or, alternatively, requesting the court to allow an exemption from surrender.

World.title: Lotteries for Telangana govt’s affordable flats in Hyderabad from August 27; draws to be livestreamed
World.content:
The lottery draws to select beneficiaries for 7,340 Indiramma Houses in Hyderabad (CURE) region would be held constituency-wise from August 27, 2026. The process would be streamed live on YouTube and other platforms.

The lotteries would be held in the presence of officials from Revenue, Housing departments and media personnel, for four constituencies everyday, said the Housing Board’s Vice Chairman V.P. Gautham.

The draws will be held according to reservations for applicants from Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), Backward Classes (BC), people with disabilities, and government outsourcing, class IV employees and sanitation workers. A waiting list for each of the categories too would be prepared and they too would be selected through lottery.

Affordable flats in towers

The State government received over 60,000 applications for 7,340 affordable flats in 16 Assembly constituencies in Core Urban Region (CURE) limits from July 21 to August 15, 2026. The affordable flats would be provided in housing towers. The government would provide a subsidy of ₹5 lakh per flat and each beneficiary has to pay ₹6 lakh in installments. While the built up area of each flat is 528 sft, carpet area is 400 sft including hall, kitchen and a bedroom.

Verification underway

Currently, verification of applications is underway. If applicants own a flat or plot within Outer Ring Road (ORR) limits, whether they have been residing in Hyderabad, and other aspects are being checked, said Mr. Gautham.

Applicants list from August 21 evening

The list of applicants would be displayed online on the websites of MeeSeva ( https://ts.meeseva.telangana.gov.in/ ), Telangana Housing Board ( tghb.cgg.gov.in , tghb.telangana.gov.in ), from the evening on Thursday (August 20, 2026).

Objections

People can submit objections against details in the list till the evening on Sunday (August 23, 2026). After examining the objections, a list of applicants eligible for the lotteries would be announced on August 25, 2026. In case of doubts, people can dial 040 24603572.
