The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Blockchain may ease cross-border liquidity, SME financing — Liminal Custody
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 25. Blockchain-based solutions could help address cross-border liquidity constraints, improve collateral mobility and facilitate institutional investment in emerging markets, Rajesh Sabari, Chief Commercial Officer at Liminal Custody, said, Trend’s special correspondent reports from Tashkent.

He made the remarks during the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum.

According to Sabari, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and the B2B segment continue to face constraints related primarily to compliance and anti-money laundering (AML) requirements. “With the emergence of regulated stablecoin issuers and fully reserve-backed instruments such as Circle, we are seeing increased traction. However, the ‘last mile’ challenge in terms of cross-border liquidity in emerging markets has yet to be fully addressed,” he said.

Sabari noted that the actual cost of a cross-border transaction should be assessed across its entire chain rather than based solely on the advertised onshore fee. “When working with regulated payment service providers, pre-transaction screening, sanctions screening, AML controls and compliance with the Travel Rule need to be embedded into the transaction chain,” he said.

He also highlighted potential applications of blockchain for institutional participants, including banks, financial institutions, traditional trustees and capital market players.

According to Sabari, for these institutions the initial use case may be less about cross-border payments and more about improving collateral mobility, as significant amounts of capital can be pre-funded and remain locked up. “This is where blockchain can provide greater asset mobility. For example, tokenized debt instruments, which most treasurers hold, can be moved much faster and deployed through programmable logic,” he said.

Another potential application is SME lending in emerging markets, particularly by providing foreign institutional investors with greater access to local assets.

Sabari said that entering emerging markets can involve significant administrative and other barriers, while blockchain could facilitate the placement of identity and other relevant information on-chain. “This does not mean that blockchain immediately eliminates all liquidity concerns. However, it makes it easier to bring identity and other relevant data on-chain, helping reduce the risk premium that institutional investors assign to foreign assets,” he said.

He added that Liminal Custody is focused on bringing institutional policy controls, including whitelisting, key management and asset segregation, onto blockchain-based infrastructure. “The goal is to provide on-chain a framework comparable to the one they operate under within a banking charter or payment service provider license,” Sabari said.

World.title: Uzbekistan develops new microfinance bank format - tayanch (Exclusive)
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 25. Uzbekistan is continuing the digitalization of financial services, while a new type of financial institution — the microfinance bank — has emerged in the country's market.

Vladislav Kim, head of the project office at TAYANCH MIKROMOLIYA BANKI JSC, told Trend's special correspondent on the sidelines of the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum in Tashkent.

According to Vladislav, the digitalization of Uzbekistan's financial sector is continuing actively in 2026 and encompasses banks, microfinance organizations and fintech companies.

"Financial services in Uzbekistan are continuing to be actively digitized and integrated into ecosystems. Alongside traditional financial services, banks and payment organizations are actively integrating everyday services such as insurance, marketplaces and others. The Central Bank is also preparing regulations for Islamic banking," Vladislav said.

He also spoke about the emergence of a new microfinance bank status in Uzbekistan. Previously, banks and microfinance organizations held licenses to provide relevant financial services, but microfinance organizations had limited opportunities to integrate with certain payment systems and processing infrastructure.

"Not long ago, a resolution was issued allowing microfinance organizations to apply for microfinance bank status," he said.

According to Vladislav, the requirements for obtaining this status differ from those applicable to conventional banks, while providing microfinance organizations with a broader range of opportunities.

He said TAYANCH MIKROMOLIYA BANKI JSC was the first and, currently, the only institution in Uzbekistan to receive the status.

Tayanch currently provides a broad range of financial services to individuals, self-employed people, individual entrepreneurs and legal entities, with a particular focus on supporting small businesses.

"Tayanch is actively promoting products and services for individual entrepreneurs and self-employed people, creating favorable conditions for the launch and development of small businesses," Vladislav said.

According to him, the bank plans to offer small businesses not only financial services in the future, but also consulting on accounting and other business-related matters directly through the Tayanch app.

"At Tayanch, we are building services aimed at making our customers' lives easier and saving their valuable time," he said.

Vladislav added that the bank also serves individual customers, offering both online channels and traditional services through its branches.

World.title: Second day of Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum kicks off in Tashkent (PHOTO)
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 25. The Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum continued its work in Tashkent.

The second day of the large-scale event focuses on the practical implementation of digital currencies, the development of cross-border fintech corridors and the expansion of investment cooperation across the Silk Road region, Trend’s special correspondent reports.

The forum is organized by the Central Bank of Uzbekistan jointly with Singapore-based international network Global Finance & Technology Network (GFTN).

The event has brought together more than 6,000 participants and around 200 speakers from 74 countries, including heads of regulatory bodies, representatives of relevant ministries, international financial institutions and investors with a combined assets under management of more than $4 billion.

During the key sessions on the second day, delegates and experts are discussing practical steps toward transitioning from traditional banking to digital financial ecosystems, the development of Open Banking, as well as regulatory frameworks for stablecoins and central bank digital currencies (CBDCs).

Key topics include the launch of the Uzbek regulator’s updated international Regulatory Sandbox 2.0, venture capital programs and legislative initiatives in Islamic finance.

Participants will also focus on cybersecurity and personal data protection amid the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in the financial sector, as well as creating a favorable environment for attracting international technology startups.

Will be updated

World.title: Uzbekistan’s TMK explores new export opportunities in South Korea
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Uzbekistan Technological Metals Complex (TMK) is exploring opportunities to expand exports to South Korea and strengthen industrial cooperation with Korean companies.

This was reflected in the statement by the TMK, following the Uzbekistan-Korea Business Forum in Tashkent.

The forum brought together representatives of the Korea Importers Association (KOIMA), the South Korean Embassy in Uzbekistan, KOTRA, the Foreign Investment Promotion Agency and Korean businesses to discuss opportunities to expand trade, investment and industrial cooperation between the two countries.

Timur Khikmatullaev, director of the Department of International Economic Relations and Diplomatic Cooperation at TMK, addressed the forum’s main session, presenting the company’s operations, export potential and priority areas for international cooperation.

As part of the event, TMK representatives held B2B meetings with GS Global Corp. and TM International Co., Ltd.The discussions focused on opportunities to supply TMK products to the Korean market, establish new trade ties and expand bilateral cooperation.

“Participation in international business platforms provides TMK with additional opportunities to enter new export markets, establish technological partnerships and expand the production of high-value-added products based on Uzbekistan’s critical mineral resources,” the company said.

South Korea is a major global hub for high-tech manufacturing, automotive production and advanced industrial technologies, creating potential opportunities for cooperation with Uzbekistan’s emerging critical minerals sector.

TMK said further engagement with Korean companies could support the expansion of its export geography, development of new industrial partnerships and deeper integration into international value chains.

World.title: 1.6 million attempts to connect to the network using duplicated IMEI codes
World.content:
“AzInTelecom” LLC, a company within AZCON Holding, continues to take measures against the registration of mobile devices imported into Azerbaijan using fraudulent IMEI codes.

As part of these measures, 77,614 copied IMEI codes have so far been assigned “clone” status and blocked. Investigations have revealed that, to date, 1,613,177 attempts have been made to connect to mobile networks in Azerbaijan using duplicated IMEI codes. All such attempts were detected and prevented by the Mobile Device Registration System (MDRS) operated by “AzInTelecom”.

Under the “Rules for the Registration of Mobile Devices,” approved by a decision of the Cabinet of Ministers, the IMEI codes of mobile devices brought into Azerbaijan from abroad must be registered within 30 days for the devices to be used on the country’s telecommunications networks. Registration can be completed online via the mygov portal or in person at post offices.

Efforts to prevent the registration of mobile devices using fraudulent IMEI codes help protect subscribers’ rights and ensure transparency in the mobile communications market. “AzInTelecom” LLC recommends that citizens check the IMEI number indicated on the device packaging via the mygov portal before purchasing a mobile phone and give preference to reputable retailers.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Azeri Light oil price eases to $95.13 per barrel
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. The price of Azerbaijan's Azeri Light crude on a CIF basis at the Italian port of Augusta fell by $1.99, or 2.1%, from the previous level to $95.13 per barrel.

The information was provided by oil market participants.

"The price of Azerbaijan's Azeri Light crude on an FOB basis at the Turkish port of Ceyhan fell by $2.08, or 2.2%, to $91.62 per barrel. The price of URALS crude declined by $1.88, or 2.7%, from the previous level to $68.41 per barrel. The price of North Sea Dated Brent fell by $1.83, or 1.9%, to $92.60 per barrel," the information said.

Azerbaijan's 2026 state budget is based on an average oil price of $65 per barrel.

Brent crude steadied above $92 per barrel on Tuesday after declining in the previous session, as the United States intensified economic pressure on Iran and its trading partners, with China reportedly not exempt from the measures.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington plans to isolate Iran through sanctions targeting entities and individuals doing business with the country. He said the objective was to cut off Tehran's economic lifelines, although the scope of further measures remains uncertain.

Brent crude fell more than 2% to below $93 per barrel on Monday, ending a two-week rally as traders awaited details of the U.S. plan to intensify pressure on Iran.

Targeting China, the largest buyer of Iranian crude, could increase pressure on Tehran but also pose risks to the broader global economy. Iran has previously demonstrated its ability to circumvent sanctions and has warned countries against supporting Washington's efforts.

Meanwhile, oil continues to move through the Strait of Hormuz, with shipments remaining relatively strong despite ongoing geopolitical risks. Reports indicated that around 16 million barrels crossed the waterway in a single night last week, although flows can vary significantly.
