World.title: Uzbekistan’s investment boom: Can capital deliver sustainable growth?
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 25. Uzbekistan is accelerating its investment drive as the government seeks to expand industrial capacity, attract foreign capital and deepen the role of private investment in the economy. With 338.9 trillion soums ($28.6 billion) invested in fixed capital in the first half of 2026, a 17.5% year-on-year increase, and $32.9 billion in foreign investments and loans utilized in the period from January through July, the scale of capital formation is becoming a defining feature of the country's growth model.

The government is now moving beyond simply attracting investment. It is attempting to build the financial, industrial and human-capital infrastructure needed to turn inflows of capital into higher productivity, stronger exports and sustainable economic growth.

This shift is increasingly visible in the composition of investment. Manufacturing, construction and energy-related activities accounted for nearly half of fixed-capital investment in the first half of the year, while the government is simultaneously preparing new industrial and infrastructure projects worth billions of dollars and expanding companies' access to international capital markets.

However, the key question is whether Uzbekistan will be able to turn this investment boom into long-term productive capacity, rather than simply an increase in capital inflows.

Investment becomes a central pillar of growth

Uzbekistan's investment expansion is taking place against a backdrop of sustained economic growth.

Speaking at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov said average annual GDP growth had remained around 6–7%, while the economy had tripled in nominal terms from approximately $60 billion to $180 billion.

The country's economic expansion has been accompanied by improving macroeconomic indicators. Kuchkarov said inflation, which had previously remained in double digits, is expected to reach around 6.5% this year, with the government targeting the 5% level next year. External public debt has remained around 27% of GDP, while budget deficits have stayed below 3% of GDP in recent years.

This combination of relatively rapid growth and improving macroeconomic stability is important for investors. A predictable macroeconomic environment reduces some of the risks associated with long-term projects, particularly in infrastructure and manufacturing, where investment returns often depend on conditions over many years.

At the same time, Uzbekistan is seeking to improve its sovereign credit standing, complete accession to the World Trade Organization, and further reduce the state's role in the economy.

These reforms suggest that the government sees foreign investment not as a temporary source of financing, but as part of a broader transition toward a more market-oriented economic model.

Manufacturing is at the heart of the investment drive

The distribution of fixed-capital investment in the first half of 2026 provides an important indication of where Uzbekistan's growth strategy is heading.

Manufacturing attracted 100.5 trillion soums ($8.5 billion), making it by far the largest recipient and accounting for almost 30% of total fixed-capital investment.

Agriculture, forestry and fisheries followed with 32.9 trillion soums ($2.7 billion), while construction attracted 32.5 trillion soums ($2.7 billion).

Electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply received 29.9 trillion soums ($2.5 billion), residential construction accounted for 27.3 trillion soums ($2.3 billion), and mining and quarrying attracted 21.8 trillion soums ($1.9 billion).

Transportation and storage received another 16.3 trillion soums ($1.4 billion).

Taken together, manufacturing, construction and energy-related activities attracted approximately 162.9 trillion soums ($13.8 billion), or about 48% of all fixed-capital investment during the first half of the year.

The concentration is significant. It suggests that Uzbekistan is prioritizing sectors that can directly expand physical production capacity and address infrastructure constraints.

Manufacturing investment alone was more than three times the amount allocated to agriculture, forestry and fisheries, the second-largest recipient.

For Uzbekistan, this could support a gradual transition from an economy reliant on commodity production and domestic demand toward one with a larger industrial and export-oriented base.

But the size of investment will not by itself determine whether that transition succeeds. The critical issue will be whether new factories and infrastructure generate sufficient productivity gains, exports and local value creation.

$27 billion project pipeline signals continued expansion

The investment drive is also being reinforced by a large pipeline of new projects.

Uzbekistan plans to launch 105 industrial and infrastructure projects worth $27 billion this year, covering energy, transport, manufacturing, logistics and urban development.

Among the major projects are a nuclear power plant in Jizzakh, a fourth copper processing plant in Almalyk, new highways connecting Tashkent with Samarkand and Andijan, an environmentally friendly aviation-fuel complex in Khorezm, a large greenhouse complex in Surkhandarya and the New Tashkent airport in Yukori Chirchiq.

The scale and diversity of these projects illustrate an important feature of Uzbekistan's investment strategy: capital is being directed simultaneously toward production, energy security, transport connectivity and urban infrastructure.

This matters because infrastructure bottlenecks could otherwise constrain the country's rapid economic expansion.

Electricity and gas supply attracted almost $2.5 billion in fixed investment during the first half of 2026, while transportation and storage received around $1.4 billion. These investments can provide the underlying infrastructure required for industrial expansion.

The challenge is to ensure that infrastructure investment remains closely linked to productive economic activity rather than creating excess capacity or placing unnecessary pressure on public finances.

The next stage: bringing private companies to international capital markets

One of the most significant developments in Uzbekistan's investment strategy is the government's attempt to diversify the sources of corporate financing.

Uzbekistan aims to attract at least $1 billion in foreign capital annually through IPOs, creating an alternative to traditional bank lending.

The initiative follows the listing of a 30% stake in the National Investment Fund, which holds assets in 13 strategic companies, on the Tashkent and London stock exchanges.

The government plans to select 50 companies each year with annual revenues exceeding 1 trillion soums for an IPO acceleration program. It will cover half of the costs associated with preparing companies for listings and bringing their financial reporting into line with international standards.

This could become an important structural change for Uzbekistan's economy.

The country's investment boom has so far relied heavily on large projects, bank financing and foreign investment. Developing equity markets could broaden access to capital and allow successful domestic companies to finance expansion without relying exclusively on bank loans.

The policy is also consistent with the government's wider objective of reducing the state's presence in the economy.

If more Uzbek companies become capable of raising capital internationally, the result could be greater corporate transparency, stronger financial reporting and increased participation by institutional investors.

However, turning the initiative into a sustainable source of foreign capital will require Uzbek companies to strengthen transparency, corporate governance and financial reporting while demonstrating strong growth potential to international investors.

The banking system is also being redirected toward smaller businesses

While the government is developing equity markets for larger companies, it is simultaneously attempting to improve access to finance for small and medium-sized businesses.

The share of small businesses in banks' loan portfolios has increased from 45% to 63%, while 76.5 trillion soums ($6.4 billion) was allocated to SMEs during the first half of 2026.

A new digital portal allows entrepreneurs to submit a single credit application while banks compete to provide financing. New entrepreneurs can apply online for loans of up to 5 billion soums (about $423,026).

The government is also introducing three programs — Business Start, Business Lift and Business Rise — designed to support businesses at different stages of development.

Under Business Start, entrepreneurs will receive assistance with project development, loan documentation and financial reporting, including through artificial intelligence. The program will have 100 billion soums ($8.4 million) in funding and offer ready-made business plans and unsecured loans of up to 200 million soums (around $16,921).

This approach is important because a sustainable investment economy cannot rely exclusively on large foreign-funded projects.

The development of domestic SMEs is necessary to create local suppliers, services and employment around major investment projects. If small businesses can scale into larger companies, the benefits of foreign investment could spread further through the domestic economy.

Human capital may become the next investment bottleneck

One of the more important aspects of Uzbekistan's current investment policy is the growing emphasis on skills.

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has highlighted the need to link investment in advanced technologies with workforce development, noting that Uzbekistan is implementing $50 billion worth of high-tech investment projects annually and that training must form part of such projects.

This is an important consideration because the productivity gains from foreign investment depend not only on the arrival of new equipment or technology, but also on the ability of local workers to operate and maintain it.

A vocational training model based on German and Chinese experience has already been introduced in Urgench, covering professions including green energy, construction, nursing, agronomy and electrical engineering.

The government aims to train 1 million young people in modern professions and help them secure higher-paying jobs.

For an economy experiencing rapid industrialization, this could be decisive.

Uzbekistan can attract factories, power plants and infrastructure projects relatively quickly. Building a workforce capable of supporting increasingly sophisticated industries takes considerably longer.

A shortage of skilled workers could therefore become a constraint on the country's ability to absorb foreign technology and move into higher-value manufacturing.

Logistics is another piece of the investment equation

Uzbekistan's investment strategy is also increasingly linked to its ambition to become a regional logistics hub.

The government has abolished import duties and recycling fees on trucks and plans to reduce VAT on the provision of railway wagons for international transportation to zero.

A logistics center with a capacity of 500,000 tons is expected to begin operations at Georgia's Poti port next year, while work on the Anaklia port project is also planned.

Major logistics hubs are planned in Alat, Termez, Yangiyul, Akhangaran and Khanabad.

For a landlocked country, improvements in logistics can have an economic impact extending far beyond the transport sector. Lower transportation costs and improved access to international markets can make Uzbek manufacturing more competitive and encourage foreign companies to use the country as a production base.

The development of transport links therefore complements investment in manufacturing.

A factory can increase production, but without efficient access to export markets its potential remains limited.

Azerbaijan-Uzbekistan investment cooperation adds another dimension

The growing scale of Uzbekistan's investment needs is also creating opportunities for bilateral investment partnerships.

During the third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, President Ilham Aliyev said the projects already envisioned and contracted between the two countries significantly exceed the capacity of the $500 million Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan Investment Fund.

According to Aliyev, around $160 million of the fund had already been allocated, while the overall portfolio of projects is considerably larger.

He specifically pointed to plans for approximately $5 billion in investment in Uzbekistan's tourism sector alone, in addition to hotel and residential projects in Tashkent that fall outside the investment fund's current scope.

The comments indicate that the existing investment mechanism may need to expand if bilateral projects continue to grow.

More importantly, the Uzbekistan-Azerbaijan example illustrates how foreign investment is increasingly moving beyond individual projects toward broader investment ecosystems involving funds, infrastructure, tourism, logistics and real estate.

For Uzbekistan, diversified bilateral investment partnerships can provide additional sources of capital while reducing dependence on any single investor or financing channel.

The diversification question

Despite the positive momentum, Uzbekistan's investment figures also reveal areas where diversification could go further.

Investment remains heavily concentrated in manufacturing, construction, energy, mining and infrastructure.

By comparison, sectors such as finance, healthcare, information and communications, professional services and other knowledge-intensive activities attracted substantially smaller amounts.

Financial and insurance activities received only 2.4 trillion soums (about $203 million), while information and communications attracted 5.8 trillion soums (around $490.7 million), and healthcare and social services received 4.6 trillion soums (approx. $389.1 million).

This does not necessarily indicate weakness. In a rapidly industrializing economy, infrastructure and manufacturing naturally require substantial capital.

However, as Uzbekistan's physical infrastructure expands, the next stage of growth could require greater investment in digital technologies, financial services, healthcare, education, professional services and other high-value sectors.

Greater diversification would also make the economy less dependent on capital-intensive industries.

The real test is what happens after the investment arrives

Uzbekistan has already demonstrated that it can attract substantial capital.

The more difficult question is whether the investment will generate sufficient economic returns.

The country's 17.5% increase in fixed-capital investment, $32.9 billion in utilized foreign investments and loans during January-July, and a $27 billion project pipeline demonstrate strong investor and government activity.

But the ultimate success of the strategy will depend on several factors.

First, new projects must generate higher productivity and exports, rather than simply increasing domestic capacity.

Second, foreign investment needs to create stronger links with Uzbek companies through local procurement, technology transfer, and workforce development.

Third, the expansion of capital markets must give successful domestic businesses access to financing beyond bank credit.

Fourth, investment in infrastructure must keep pace with industrial expansion.

And finally, the country must continue strengthening macroeconomic stability and regulatory predictability.

Uzbekistan's government appears increasingly aware of this shift. Its policies now connect investment with privatization, IPOs, SME financing, logistics, vocational education, and international market integration.

That suggests the country is moving from an investment-attraction model toward an investment-conversion model.

The objective is no longer simply to bring more dollars into Uzbekistan. It is to turn those dollars into factories, exports, technology, skilled workers, competitive domestic companies, and higher incomes.

The scale of investment now being mobilized allows Uzbekistan to accelerate its transformation into a more diversified and productive economy.

But the size of the opportunity also raises the stakes.

The success of Uzbekistan's investment boom will ultimately be measured not by how much capital enters the country, but by how effectively that capital changes what the economy produces, exports and earns.

World.title: Darwin retirees lose home and all possessions in Livingstone fire
World.content:
As he sifts through the debris looking for his glasses and wife's engagement ring, Graham Doyle only finds rubble and dust.

He is back at the place he called home for 32 years, a day after a fire swept through the Livingstone property on Darwin's outskirts on Sunday afternoon.

"We've lost our house. There is nothing left," he said.

Graham Doyle and his wife Margaret lived in their home for more than 30 years. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

Mr Doyle and his wife, Margaret, were at home watching the football and getting ready to prepare dinner when Margaret noticed the smell of smoke.

The last time a fire alert was issued the blaze was moving away from their home. But looking out the back door this time, Mr Doyle saw the flames racing towards them.

The couple had just minutes to act.

Firefighting crews captured the scale of the fire that swept through the rural area, on the outskirts of Darwin. (Supplied: CMC Secure NT )

"It was like the surf coming in on the East Coast. It just flew down … travelled 350 metres in about a minute," Mr Doyle said.

"I've never seen anything move that fast. I don't know how to describe it other than absolutely terrifying."

Mr Doyle said they had no time to save any precious belongings, but managed to race their three beloved dogs outside to safety.

"I came back in abundantly trying to put the fire out," he said.

"The garden hose burnt through, so that was useless.

"I grabbed a couple of buckets and went to the kitchen sink.

"There was a fireball that hit me, and that was basically the last I could do in the house."

The fire burnt through the house leaving only some china cups as survivors in the kitchen. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

High fuel load contributed to fire intensity, Incident Controller says

Bushfires NT Incident Controller Nathaniel Staniford confirmed only one house was severely impacted by Sunday's fire, and said the high fuel load in the area contributed to the intensity and spread of the blaze.

Iconic Top End national park under threat from invasive grass Bringing in more than 250,000 visitors a year, Litchfield National Park has become one of the Northern Territory's star attractions but it's under threat from a near-invisible invader.

"There were several properties where the fire did break containment lines," he said.

"Those properties did contain gamba [grass] on them and that did help the fire to spread rapidly."

He said additional crews were called in to help once it was clear the fire could impact multiple properties, because Bushfires NT crews don't have the training or equipment to enter burning buildings.

While fire trucks turned up to help, Mr Doyle said they ran out of water.

Graham and his wife had to flee their home on Sunday and say they didn't have any time to save their belongings. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

"Watching, it was like the house was the timber inside a wood fire stove and the flames were just jumping up everywhere," he said.

Mr Doyle was taken to hospital with minor burns and smoke inhalation.

While he has lost nearly everything, he said he was lucky to be alive.

He returned on Tuesday to the destruction of his home wearing donated clothes and shoes to search for their irreplaceable items.

"My wife's engagement ring and wedding ring, they are somewhere down in amongst the rubble. She didn't get to get them out and I was trying to put the fire out in her room so I could get those for her," he said.

"My parents' medals … My parents' army discharge certificates, all of my university and TAFE qualifications are gone."

The majority of Graham and Margaret's belongings burnt in the fire. (ABC News: Roxanne Fitzgerald )

While a crowdfunding campaign set up by their grand-daughter has so far raised more than $8,000, the couple now face the daunting task of rebuilding their lives and finding somewhere permanent to live.

Graham also said due to historical storm water drainage issues in the area, the couple was unable to insure their home.

"The only thing we can think of at the moment is to try and get a cheap caravan."

World.title: Richmond denies players 'making light' of Swans scandal on Mad Monday
World.content:
The Richmond Football Club has denied its players were "referencing or making light of recent matters" in footage recorded during their post-season celebrations.

Tiger players were recorded during a drinking session at a Victorian country pub, with one player seen feigning shock after being spanked on his rear by a teammate.

Another teammate whips a fellow player on the back with a belt in footage captured by news outlets on Monday, leading to speculation they were referencing the ongoing Sydney Swans scandal.

The club denied that was the case.

"Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end of season gathering," a statement read.

"The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.

"The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters."

Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony AFL boss Andrew Dillon speaks to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

The Tigers finished second last this season with a 3-20 win-loss record.

The pub that hosted Richmond's drinks said the controversy had been blown out of proportion.

"In our view, this has been blown out of proportion," the Garfield Hotel, 80 kilometres east of Melbourne, said in a statement posted on social media.

The hotel said it "could not speak more highly" of how players behaved.

"For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with," the statement read.

Nick Blakey (left) is one of the Swans suspended for breaching club standards. (AAP Image: Dean Lewins)

"They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that.

"They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site.

"They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on."

The hotel noted media were waiting for the Tigers players "in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing".

The Richmond footage emerged hours after AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon fronted the media for the first time since the Swans scandal began.

"I have been asked a lot in recent days, what message football should be sending young people and what we should be saying to our kids," Dillon said.

"For me, the answer is straightforward: it doesn't matter who you are, it doesn't matter what you do, whether you're an AFL footballer — the way we treat women says a lot about who we are as people, as a community and as a game.

"Quite simply, respect for women is not negotiable."

Dillon said the actions of the five suspended Swans players had "fallen well short of the standards our game expects and community deserves".

"While there are players involved, we cannot lose sight of the bigger picture. More importantly, there are women who have made a report to police and they should be shown care and respect," he said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Man accused of making deepfakes of students told police it was 'like X-ray vision'
World.content:
A man accused of making sexualised deepfake images of former Brisbane high school students and staff told police he did it because it was "funny" and described it as being akin to "X-ray vision glasses", a jury has heard.

Antonio Rotondo pleaded not guilty in the Brisbane District Court to more than a dozen charges, including 11 counts of stalking and five counts of distributing intimate images.

He is also fighting one charge of distributing child exploitation material.

Crown prosecutor Ben Jackson told the jury in September 2023, when Mr Rotondo was living in the Philippines, he sent an email containing numerous images to several recipients, including two Brisbane private schools.

Mr Rotondo has been charged with 11 counts of stalking and five counts of distributing intimate images. (ABC News)

Mr Jackson told the jury the images depicted current and former female students and staff at one of the schools which had been "altered in a digital way".

"To either remove some of their clothing entirely, or to replace that clothing with very revealing lingerie," he said.

The jury heard he did the same thing with images of various models who had been part of Brisbane Fashion Week and sent those to another woman involved in that event.

He also uploaded 16 of the deepfake images to a website that he ran, the jury heard.

Mr Jackson told the jury the feelings of complainants were not ordinarily relevant to an offence at trial, but in this case, they would be.

He said jurors would only need to determine that the offending would "cause someone in normal circumstances some distress".

"[The complainants] will tell you in their own words how they felt," he said.

The jury heard Mr Rotondo spoke with police in the days after he arrived in Australia in October 2023.

Mr Jackson told the jury he gave them "a full and frank set of statements" in a recorded interview.

"Which the crown says amount to admissions … that would count against him in his criminal trial," he said.

The jury heard Mr Rotondo told police he was the user of the email account and accepted he had sent the images and he controlled the website where they were uploaded.

He also admitted he had altered the images using a website, the jury heard.

Jury hears accused told police 'it's funny'

Mr Jackson told the jury in the police interview, which will be played during the trial, Mr Rotondo told officers making deepfakes was "just a hobby".

He said Mr Rotondo explained he did it because it was "just the type of person" he was.

"I'm at the stage of my life where I really don't care, I think it's funny," he said Mr Rotondo told police.

"I don't know the people … never met them, never will meet them."

Mr Jackson told the jury Mr Rotondo also stated in his police interview "you cannot stop deepfakes" and "everyone should live in fear" of them.

"Every woman on earth should live in fear of a camera," he said Mr Rotondo told police.

"You cannot stop it … I know the laws are trying to stop it in Australia, but it will not stop."

" From a guy point of view, from a practical point of view, it's fun to just press a button and remove their clothes, it's like X-ray vision glasses. "

"If there are services that exist that do it … and there's software that's available that makes it possible, it's acceptable to a percentage of community to make deepfakes."

The trial continues.

World.title: NSW prison officers strike over colleague's alleged assault by inmate
World.content:
New South Wales prison officers have walked off the job in protest after an inmate accused of brutally assaulting one of their colleagues was released from custody.

The union representing corrections officers has supplied a picture which it said showed the injuries sustained by the officer at the John Moroney Correctional Centre near Windsor several weeks ago.

The Public Services Association of NSW (PSA) said the attack left the officer with a broken eye socket, broken nose and missing teeth.

The PSA said the inmate was granted bail on other matters and was initially not charged over the alleged assault.

On Tuesday afternoon, NSW Police said in a statement the 55-year-old corrections officers was allegedly attacked by a 21-year-old inmate on July 25.

The man was arrested at a home on Lloyd Street in Blacktown about 11am on Tuesday.

He was taken to Blacktown police station where he was charged with causing grievous bodily harm to a law enforcement officer.

He was refused bail to appear at Blacktown Local Court on Tuesday.

'Members are livid'

PSA general secretary Stewart Little said prisoners had been locked down in their cells and trucks were bringing prisoners involved in court proceedings back to prison.

"Our members are livid. A corrections officers gets bashed and left with life changing injuries and the guy gets released back into the community without being charged? That's outrageous," Mr Little said before the man was charged on Tuesday.

A spokeswoman for Corrective Services NSW said the alleged assault remained a NSW Police investigation.

"Any decisions regarding charges are matters for police," she said.

"Staff are right to expect that inmates who assault them in the workplace will be met with the full force of the law and we encourage staff on duty to remain at work whilst police investigate."

The spokeswoman said the 24-hour walk-out has been referred to the Industrial Relations Commission.

"All correctional centres remain secure and appropriate care and essential services continue to be provided for inmates," she said.

"Corrective Services NSW is continuing to support the injured officer who, like all staff deserves to be safe at work."

World.title: Darwin Woolworths blasts jingle outside store to stop 'loitering'
World.content:
Woolworths is blasting its Fresh Food People jingle at its Darwin city store in the hopes it will stop loitering and anti-social behaviour directed at staff and customers.

The supermarket giant has recently installed several outdoor speakers that play the 20-second song on a loop, which can be heard from across the street.

The supermarket sits across the road from a university campus, near residential apartments and next to a major bus stop with the music also audible there.

The store is located right next to a popular bus stop in the CBD. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Some have described the jingle as "very irritating" and "constant" with one customer saying, "it drives me nuts".

"It's not annoying me but it's on repeat, all the time," another shopper told the ABC.

Music aims to tackle anti-social behaviour

A spokesperson for Woolworths said the system was introduced earlier this month to tackle safety concerns, after the store reported 24 incidents of violent or aggressive behaviour this year.

Woolworths says the jingle is being played on a loop in hopes of discouraging anti-social behaviour. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"We've received numerous complaints from the community and our own Woolworths team members about their safety while entering and exiting our Darwin City store," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"This is due to ongoing issues of anti-social behaviour and aggression from individuals loitering outside in the carpark and at the bus stop for extended periods of time.

"We introduced a music speaker system that discourages loitering, helping to increase safety."

The tactic is not being used by any other Woolworths store in the country.

A spokesperson for the City of Darwin said the music was being played "from within the Woolworths premises" and none of the speakers are located on City of Darwin-controlled public land.

The tune is played over loudspeakers in the immediate area of the Darwin City Woolworths. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"Therefore, City of Darwin has no role in authorising the music being played by Woolworths," the spokesperson said.

"As the Woolworths and associated car park are not owned or controlled by City of Darwin, capacity to intervene in that space is limited, however City of Darwin will continue to assist where appropriate and within the scope of its jurisdiction."

Tactic an example of 'hostile' architecture

Woolworths isn't the first to use music as a means of tackling anti-social behaviour or driving away unwanted visitors.

In 2023, the City of Bunbury council in Western Australia came under fire for playing The Wiggles' song Hot Potato on a loop to drive homeless people away from a regularly used shelter and sleeping spot.

Wiggles 'disappointed' by council's weaponisation of Hot Potato The children's music group says the City of Bunbury's decision to play the song on a loop to stop people from sleeping rough at a public bandstand runs counter to the message of their music.

In Melbourne, Coles faced criticism for playing opera from a store in the inner-city suburb of Prahran which could be heard from the street in an attempt to deter crime.

Mark Olweny, an associate professor of architecture at Charles Darwin University, said the use of loud or repetitive music is an example of "aggressive" or "defensive" architecture.

He said while the use of "annoying" audio may be effective in the short term, the tactic could be "counterproductive" in the longer term.

"It has a downside because it doesn't only effect the people you want to move on, but it's also going to affect the people you want in that space as well," he said.

Mr Olweny said people may learn to blank out the sound and while people may be deterred temporarily, they would ultimately return for reasons like shade or transport.

Mark Olweny says the looping jingle is an example of "aggressive" or "defensive" architecture. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"In some instances, it may be called loitering but for the individual it is not loitering, they're there because there is a need that space is fulfilling," he said.

"In this case it could be getting away from the sun so if there's shade people are seeking that's where people will go."

"If we address that in a more nuanced way … or empathetic way we may find that the issue of loitering will be resolved with better outcomes rather than taking an aggressive approach."

Loading...

Northern Territory Police said there were regular patrols of the area.

"The Darwin CBD, including the area surrounding Woolworths and the bus interchange, remains an area of regular police activity due to the high volume of people moving through the location each day," a spokesperson said.

"While some incidents can involve violence, the majority of police interactions are resolved through early engagement and proactive intervention before behaviour escalates."

World.title: Construction executives' dogs poisoned during CFMEU dispute, inquiry hears
World.content:
Queensland's Commission of Inquiry into CFMEU has heard explosive allegations the union engaged private detectives to spy on security contractors.

The inquiry heard allegations one security contractor found tracking tags on their car and said his dogs was allegedly poisoned in a separate incident.

Grant Killen, the managing director of private security business Concentric Concepts, gave evidence to the inquiry today.

Mr Killen said he was engaged by contractor BMD to provide security services to its executives and the Centenary Bridge upgrade project, as the builder was in a long-running dispute with the union.

Grant Killen told the inquiry he discovered a tracking device attached to his vehicle. (Supplied)

"There were concerns about continuous CFMEU activity that may hinder or disrupt the project," Mr Killen said.

"There was a requirement for some security services."

On May 17, 2014, Mr Killen said he was driving back to his office from the project site when he had the "uneasy feeling" he was "being followed".

"Back at the office, I had a vehicle hoist and immediately lifted the vehicle," he said.

" I found a tracking device that had been installed under the vehicle. "

Mr Killen said it appeared the device had only been installed recently and he wasn't aware why someone would want to track his movements.

"I immediately put the vehicle on the ground as quickly as I could. I left the facility gave the admin staff at the office a call and directed them to pack up and close up for the day and go home," he said.

Mr Killen alleged he was followed while driving with the tracking device. (Supplied)

"My intention was to put as much distance between my staff and the actual device.

"I left the device on the vehicle, as I knew it had an anti-kill switch, so the people who had the software for that would be immediately notified the device was removed."

Mr Killen said as he was driving near the Carindale area when he noticed a white SUV following him.

"My first intention was to confirm it was following me … so I conducted some aggressive driving," he said.

"That included going through a red light … I was followed through that red light.

The device Mr Killen found on his vehicle. (Supplied)

"Further down the road I did an aggressive U-turn … it followed."

Mr Killen said he then aggressively hit the brakes and brought the vehicle closer to him to try and get a look at the driver, but at that time the car left.

He took the car to an area unrelated to him or his family in Bulimba, parked it and then went to the police.

"[The next day] I went back to the area where I disposed of the [car]," he said.

"I was a bit surprised when I did turn up there that the device was there.

"I did pick it up to look to see if there was a sim card, which there wasn't. I observed it to be quite heavily damaged."

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC. (Supplied)

Multiple dogs poisoned

Around the time of these disputes, Mr Killen said he also noticed drones flying near his home.

It was at that time he had to take his dog to the vet as the animal became sick.

"I formed the opinion there was the possibility the dog had been baited," he said.

Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC asked Mr Killen is if suspected the drones might have dropped the baited meat.

"Correct," he responded.

He said others associated with the Centenary Bridge upgrade project, BMD executive Mick Power, also had dogs poisoned after seeing drones around their properties.

Mick Power's son, Scott Power, the now CEO of BMD, said at the time his father's dog was poisoned, the CFMEU had been running a targeted campaign in the streets around the home.

He said while he didn't know who poisoned the dog, the timing coincided with the CFMEU's campaign, and drones had not been seen around the home before that time or since.

"[My parents] thought it was connected," he said.

BMD boss Scott Power told the inquiry his father's dog was poisoned. (Supplied)

Earlier on Tuesday, the inquiry was shown evidence the CFMEU had engaged former police detective Mick Featherstone as a private investigator to conduct research into BMD executives.

Mr Killen said he noticed Mr Featherstone outside his house one day.

"I did observe a number of vehicles [near] my house," he said.

"One did a U-turn in my driveway and stood there for a while. I saw him from an elevated position from my house, yes."

The ABC is not alleging Mr Featherstone is responsible for installing the tracking device on Mr Killen's car, following him on May 17 or poisoning his dog.

Concentric Concepts is one of two security organisations employed to work on the Centenary Bridge upgrade site.

The other, HOST Group, was last week the focus of scrutiny after its boss Gary Samuel, allegedly brought members of the Comancheros to the construction site, where one made threats to a CFMEU delegate.

Mr Killen told the inquiry that he was told by some security workers on the site that the CFMEU were being supported by the Bandidos.

CFMEU and bikie gang recap The latest block of hearings into the Queensland branch of the CFMEU focused on the Comanchero motorcycle gang.

But Mr Killen did not know anything further in relation to the involvement in the project by the Bandidos or Comancheros.

He said he withdrew from the Centenary Bridge Upgrade project around the time of the dog poisonings, to protect his family and staff, but throughout 2024 continued to provide protection to BMD executives.

Mr Killen, who has worked in defence and private contracting across Australia and Iraq, said what he experienced here was not something he had expected to happen in Australia.

"It was certainly a challenging period of time," he said.

World.title: Mystery solved as dead man identified three years after skull found
World.content:
The remains of an itinerant man who was never reported missing have been identified more than three years after his skull was accidentally found, following a persistent police effort and DNA supplied by his estranged sister.

Edward Harold Tait was born in 1971 to Scottish parents who would later move to regional Victoria.

According to findings handed down by Tasmanian coroner Madeleine Wilson, Mr Tait's remains were found in July 2023 at a property at Clifton Beach, in southern Tasmania, while the landowner, Gregory Hunter, was clearing weeds in a gully.

While working, Mr Hunter kicked what he believed was a rock, which he then realised appeared to be a human skull.

A police investigation of the area found a small campsite made up of a rusted corrugated iron sheet covering a shallow dugout — just large enough for a person to lay flat — about 75 metres up the slope from where the skull was found.

At the site, police found two brown men's shoes — the right one containing orthotics in the heel — a shirt, keys, a lighter and a plastic bag containing two badly disintegrated business cards.

The zippo lighter found along with the humans remains at Clifton Beach, Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

The short-sleeved top found near the makeshift camp at Clifton Beach, Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

Despite missing the lower jawbone, forensic examination determined the skull was in "excellent condition", with a brown stain on the right side indicating it had been in contact with the soil for some time.

Forensic pathologists, however, were unable to determine the cause of the individual's death.

Further forensic testing by the Australian Federal Police (AFP) comparing the DNA against samples from crime scenes, convicted offenders, suspects, volunteers and items belonging to missing people was unsuccessful.

According to the coroner's report, determining the age of the remains was also proving difficult.

In May the following year, Tasmania Police released a facial reconstruction of the man, hoping that the public could help identify the person who had so far failed to appear on any state or national DNA database.

Tasmania Police released a reconstruction of Harold Tait's face in 2024, in the hope someone from the public may have identified him. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

At the time, police said they believed the remains could be from as recent as five years ago, and up to 50 years old.

The information that could be gleaned from the skull was slim: forensic analysis had determined the remains belonged to a Caucasian male, most likely with blond, brown or black hair, one of the business cards found at the camp belonged to a restaurant on Swanston Street in Melbourne, and there was no indication of violence.

Mr Tait's sister, Helen Tait, would become the vital link in helping confirm his identity.

A 'reclusive and itinerant' existence

According to information Ms Tait provided in Ms Wilson's coronial report, Mr Tait had led a difficult and wandering life.

He was born with a congenital condition which led to one leg to be shorter than the other — a cause of significant pain later on.

Following the separation of his parents, Mr Tait's early life was split between Scotland and Australia.

He would go on to lead a "reclusive and itinerant" existence, Ms Wilson noted in her report.

After becoming estranged from his sister in 1993, he went on to find himself in trouble with police across several states, facing charges relating to trespassing, begging and stealing.

A chance meeting with her brother in Melbourne in 1998 would be the last time Ms Tait would see him.

An aerial view of terrain of Goats Beach looking in direction of Clifton Beach, Tasmania, where Tasmania Police found the skull of Harold Tait. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

Shoe orthotics a key clue

By July 2024, the forensic investigation had made a breakthrough in confirming Mr Tait's identity.

Forensic Genetic Genealogy testing through the AFP's National DNA Program had identified a third-degree male relative based off a sample taken from the skull found at Clifton Beach.

Forensic data, genealogical research, "and other relevant sources" had led investigators to identify Mr Tait as the most likely source of the unidentified remains.

In January 2025, investigators contacted Ms Tait to let her know the remains of a person believed to be her brother had been found in southern Tasmania.

Ms Tait would go on to provide a DNA sample to help the investigation.

"Helen Tait was unaware that Edward had been in Tasmania and did not know of any connection between him and the state," Ms Wilson said.

She said the fact that Mr Tait's parents were Scottish, and the additional fact that he was born with one leg shorter than the other, and that one of the two matching shoes found near skull contained orthotics, "fortified" her belief the remains were him.

Ms Wilson concluded he died at or near the shelter at an unknown date.

Coroner Madeleine Wilson says she is satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the skull found at Clifton Beach is that of Edward Tait. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

In the coroner's report, Senior Constable Lucy Brown from Tasmania Police's Missing Person Unit said investigations had revealed Mr Tait had led "an extremely reclusive and transient lifestyle" in the state, and had never been reported missing.

According to Senior Constable Brown's investigation, Mr Tait had lived in hotels and men's shelters in Hobart throughout August and September 1999, and secured a rental in New Town later that month.

He last contacted Centrelink in person on November 30, 1999 and his rental agreement was terminated in March the following year.

In her report, Ms Wilson said there were no further reported sightings of Mr Tait, and the cause of his death remains unknown.

World.title: Woman stabbed, child assaulted in Melbourne CBD attack
World.content:
A man has been arrested after a woman and a child were attacked near the Victoria Police headquarters in Melbourne's CBD.

Police have been told a 10-year-old boy was assaulted on Spencer Street near the corner of La Trobe Street about 1pm.

They say a woman who was with the boy intervened and was stabbed in the upper body.

Nearby police officers arrested a 27-year-old Sunshine West man and seized a pair of scissors.

He is yet to be interviewed by police.

"It is believed the parties were not known to each other," a police spokesperson said.

The boy and the 30-year-old woman from Cowes, south-east of Melbourne, were taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries.

An investigation into the incident is continuing.

World.title: Hundreds of buyers in limbo as major Sydney developer Bathla Group collapses
World.content:
NationalNSWInsolvency Hundreds of buyers in limbo as major Sydney developer Bathla Group collapses Ellie Busby and Anthony Segaert Updated August 25, 2026 — 4:25pm ,first published 10:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of apartment buyers have been left in limbo over the collapse of a major Australian developer, further derailing the NSW government’s ambitions for hundreds of thousands of new homes. Bathla Group entered voluntary administration on Tuesday and corporate restructuring agency Teneo was appointed to oversee the company and its hundreds of related entities, including Universal Property Group and Raj & Jai Construction. Bathla Group has collapsed. Louie Douvis The collapse of the group, which last week boasted of 3500 homes, apartments or subdivision lots being under construction, will be felt the hardest in north- and south-western Sydney, which has been reshaped by the developer’s prolific greenfield builds. The collapse has left buyers who purchased off the plan in limbo, after major developments in Box Hill and Castle Hill were plagued by delays. Work on some western Sydney Bathla projects stalled in recent months, with tradesmen walking off sites and some claiming they had not been paid.



Bathla, which has built more than 15,000 homes since 1997, has expanded into regional NSW, Victoria and South Australia. Its collapse adds further pressure to the state government’s housing agenda, already struggling amid concerns about the feasibility of apartment construction west of Parramatta. Developers have warned for more than a year that rising construction and material costs, combined with high government taxes and sluggish growth in the west of the city, were making the development of new homes unviable. Bathla founder and director Bhart Bhushan said the “orderly restructure of business” was due to “a perfect storm” of declining sales, rising construction costs and the federal government’s budget. “Our first thoughts are with our employees and the customers who have put their faith in us to deliver their dream of home ownership,” he said in a post on social media. “It is my sincere hope this process can allow that to happen by working collaboratively with the administrators, our suppliers, contractors and lending partners.”



Bathla has faced significant financial problems for the past year: it had more than $3 billion in debt and was in the sights of the state’s building regulator, which had inspected its properties more than 40 times over recent months. Related Article Exclusive

City life Janice was thrilled to buy her own unit. But she has no idea if she will ever move in Building Commission NSW last week issued its associated entity, Raj & Jai Construction, and its director two fines worth $54,000 over improper conduct in working on two Schofields properties without the required insurance. Bathla chief executive Robert Loader said in a statement the company recognised it was a “difficult situation” and the appointment of administrators was “in the best interest of all stakeholders”. “The business has been through a period of declining sales and falling property prices, while construction costs have increased,” he said. “We will work constructively with the administrators to support the continued delivery of much-needed housing for western Sydney.”



Industry sources said Bathla had about 43 lenders, none of which were major banks, making it reliant on private credit. That sector has been subject to intense regulatory and commercial scrutiny after it surged into areas that banks vacated following the global financial crisis, lured by the prospect of charging riskier clients high interest rates for loans. But this year several major private credit funds have had to pause or limit withdrawals from their own financial backers amid fears the companies they had loaned money to were at risk of failing to make repayments. Marie Sinclair (left) with her mother, Sue Mancuso, and Janice Cahill, who all purchased off-the-plan units at Bathla Group’s Kembla Grange property. Wolter Peeters “The concentration of Australia’s private credit market in higher-risk real estate construction and development is where we see the greatest area for improvement for investor protection and market integrity,” warned two experts commissioned to write a report on the area last year for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. In Box Hill, a greenfield suburb on Sydney’s north-western fringe, a $19 million apartment block was due to be built by December 2024, but buyers who had purchased units off the plan in 2022 were still waiting for it to be finished.



In Castle Hill, a major apartment development languished as an abandoned partly flooded hole in the ground, which a spokesperson said was due to delays in getting a “further staged construction certificate” for the site. Further south, in the Illawarra suburb of Kembla Grange, Building Commission NSW identified defects in a series of under-construction units which were meant to be finished by December 2025. That extension date had been extended four times, and a Bathla spokesperson last week said the project was expected to be completed by October or November. Janice Cahill, who bought an apartment at the development off the plan, said last week the delays had affected her mental health. On Tuesday morning she called her real estate agent, asking what the collapse meant, and was assured the project was continuing. Marie Sinclair, whose elderly parents bought an apartment in the same building, visited the site in September and found doors with keys left unattended, graffitied walls, half-finished copper piping and multiple broken surfaces.



A NSW government spokesperson said it would work with Bathla’s administrators to understand the implications of the appointment. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: This shrimp po’ boy is the perfect Brisbane sandwich. Here’s why
World.content:
Eating outFood This shrimp po’ boy is the perfect Brisbane sandwich. Here’s why Don’t know what a po’ boy is? You need to get across it, then eat one ASAP. There’s a catch, though. Matt Shea August 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It started with a music video. Before he made sausages and taught barbecue and had kids, Steve Lind was a DJ. Not your ex-boyfriend-with-a-busted-CDJ-DJ – an actual touring DJ with singles and remixes and the rest of it. Steve Lind from Lindy’s Po Boys. Markus Ravik In 2016, Lind found himself in New Orleans. “This was when I was doing a lot of music. I went to LA and did some studio sessions and stuff like that,” he says.



“I had a guest vocalist [Fly Boi Keno] for a song and I wanted to do a music video in New Orleans. I think I spent about two weeks in each city. Real shoestring-budget stuff. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “I knew nothing about New Orleans – maybe Bourbon Street and that was it. The videographer picked me up from the airport and took me to Parkway Tavern and Bakery. “That’s where I had my first po’ boy. I was like, ‘What the hell is this?’” What the hell is a po’ boy? Originating in New Orleans in 1929 as a cheap (or free) meal for striking streetcar workers, a po’ boy is similar to a submarine sandwich but defined by a more French-leaning roll, which is similar to a traditional baguette but lighter and fluffier inside.



Typical fillings are prawns (shrimp, of course, in US parlance), roast beef and Louisiana hot sausage, and a traditional sandwich might be dressed with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise. Similar to a sub but with a more French-leaning baguette: Steve Lind’s shrimp po’ boy. Markus Ravik It’s a relatively simple sanger that was intended as a hearty, affordable stomach filler for those “poor boy” striking streetcar workers. So, what makes it so great? “It’s the simplicity of it,” Lind says. “You can even have them undressed, and a good one will be delicious. A po’ boy is like a good cheeseburger, where all the ingredients hold up and it’s balanced, not boring. But that means you have to take good care with your ingredients.” Lindy’s Po Boys



After that initial trip, Lind returned to New Orleans twice – the second time, in early 2025, specifically to research po’ boys. He then set about trying to recreate them in Brisbane. A year later, Lindy’s Po Boys was born. This column caught it on its third pop-up at Camp Hill Bowls Club earlier this month. On the menu was a pork sausage po’ boy – Lind also operates Big Bad Smallgoods, a specialty sausage company – and a shrimp po’ boy. It’s the latter we think you need to eat ASAP. Lind’s prawns are battered in a combination of plain flour, corn starch and cornflour. Markus Ravik The shrimp po’ boy



It’s been a while since I demolished a sandwich this fast. And that’s maybe because Lind has made something that’s as easy to eat as it is delicious. Let’s start with the bread. It’s made to Lind’s specs by Norman Park’s Golden K Bakery, and it’s crisp on the outside (without being banh mi crunchy) and soft and pillowy on the inside. It’s tasty, textural, moreish. “We used to toast our bread, but that of course adds a bit of time,” Lind says. “This loaf doesn’t need toasting, and it holds up well to the wrap. Every po’ boy I’ve ever had was wrapped, and once you put the hot shrimp or sausage in there, it steams the bread a little, making it softer. That’s really important.” There’s a little bit going on with the dressing. Lind uses a moderate amount of iceberg lettuce, a few slices of tomato, and Fehlbergs burger pickles. He then gives each bun a squirt of Hellmann’s mayonnaise, Heinz tomato sauce, and Louisiana Hot Sauce for “acidity and sweetness”. Each bun gets a squirt of Hellmann’s mayonnaise, Heinz tomato sauce and Louisiana Hot Sauce. Markus Ravik



For prawns, there’s nothing fancy, with Lind opting for wild-caught prawns from the supermarket, which still have a bit of flavour but their price enables him to really pile them into the roll, just as they do in New Orleans. What he has really leaned into is his prawn batter. “I talked to Ben [Kirk] from [burger restaurant] Mr Jeebus and he gave me a whole bunch of things to think about,” Lind says. “Like, if I add sugar to my batter, it’s going to make it softer, and anything with starch will make it crispier.” Lind wanted to keep it super crispy and eventually landed on a combination of plain flour, corn starch, and cornflour, for a dash of extra colour. Prepare to become a po’ boy nerd



Lind describes himself as a po’ boy nerd (to be fair, he’s constantly on social media resharing sandwich content from New Orleans), and his local recreation will likely make you a believer too. Is this the perfect sandwich? Markus Ravik In a sense, it’s the perfect sandwich – at least in terms of what we sandwich fans look for. It’s got all that texture from the fried prawns (which remain juicy inside), crispy iceberg, and precision baked bread, but then stacks of acid, and salt and sweetness from the dressings and sauces. Also, unlike a banh mi or other baguette-based sandwiches, it’s a cinch to eat. I ate one alongside the sausage po’ boy and still wanted another. Not because I was hungry, really, but because I wanted to keep the sensation rolling. But also maybe because this is the last time I’ll get to eat one for a month or two. Lindy’s Po Boys is a semi-regular pop-up, so Lind isn’t entirely sure when the next will be, although he’s currently aiming for the King’s Birthday long weekend in early October.



We want you to eat this sandwich so we’ll keep you posted. Where to get it The Lindy’s Po Boy shrimp po’ boy is $22. The pop-up typically appears at Camp Hill Bowls Club, 150 Ferguson Road, Camp Hill.

World.title: Embarrassed Tigers say Mad Monday antics did not reference Swans scandal
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Embarrassed Tigers say Mad Monday antics did not reference Swans scandal Sam McClure Updated August 25, 2026 — 4:02pm ,first published August 25, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Richmond players seen striking each other with belts in footage taken during Mad Monday celebrations have expressed embarrassment about their behaviour but denied they were mocking the scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans. The Tigers released a statement on Tuesday afternoon in which they said they had questioned the players about their conduct at the Garfield Hotel in Gippsland on Monday. “Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end of season gathering,” the statement said. “The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.



“The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters.” In one piece of vision of the Tigers’ celebration, young midfielder Josh Smillie appears to pull down his pants and feign shock as he is repeatedly struck on the backside by a teammate. A scene from Richmond’s celebrations at the Garfield Hotel. MEDIA-MODE.COM He appears to be spanked three times in the video and then after a fourth slap, reacts differently. Another Mad Monday clip shows Richmond midfielder Tim Taranto using a belt to strike a shirtless teammate. The footage emerged just a week after five Sydney players were suspended for the remainder of the season for breaches of club standards during a night of partying that ended in a hotel room at the Pullman East Melbourne.



Allegations published by the Herald Sun included that one woman, who was also in the room, had claimed she was slapped on the buttocks four times instead of the three slaps that had been agreed. Richmond players celebrate Mad Monday. MEDIA-MODE.COM Five Sydney players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – have been suspended for breaching club standards, and a separate police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at a Melbourne hotel continues. No charges have been laid and this masthead is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended Swans players. The Richmond players told the club their antics were not related to the Swans scandal at all. Richmond players outside the venue in Garfield. MEDIA-MODE.COM



Photos taken of Richmond players at the post-season celebration on Monday appear to show pints of beer lined up on a ledge, a player climbing on a teammate’s shoulders and reaching onto a roof covering, and two players outside the venue appearing to urinate against a fence. The AFL has been contacted for comment on the Mad Monday celebration. A statement was released on the Garfield Hotel’s social media accounts defending the players. “We hosted the Richmond Football Club at our venue today, and we could not speak more highly of the way they conducted themselves. For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with,” the statement read.



“They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that. They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site. They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on. “In our view, this has been blown out of proportion. Two members of the media were waiting on their arrival this morning and remained on site filming in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing.” The footage of the Tigers prompted federal Labor MP Dan Repacholi to criticise the behaviour. “Right now we need good blokes out there having the conversations around this and calling this out for what it is because this is unacceptable, and we need to make sure we do better,” he said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview The Tigers’ season finished on Saturday after their loss to Geelong. On Monday, AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon delivered a strongly worded statement at the league’s finals launch. As the Swans crisis continues, Dillon said respect for women was not negotiable. There have been several incidents over the past few years at Mad Monday celebrations – the day to mark a club’s end of season – that have sparked controversy about player behaviour.
