World.title: ‘Classic pub punch’ costs man his job after trading slurs with colleague
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal ‘Classic pub punch’ costs man his job after trading slurs with colleague Millie Muroi August 25, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Melbourne man who punched a colleague and told him his swearing about other work colleagues was “gay” after a work Christmas party has failed to regain his job after the workplace umpire ruled his sacking was valid. The Fair Work Commission found on Monday that the building maintenance officer, who had worked for the Arts Centre Melbourne since January 2020, struck a colleague – the head of venue planning – at a pub after the Christmas party in 2024. The incident occurred after a work Christmas party. Getty Images While employers generally have limited right to control employees’ behaviour outside work hours, Monday’s decision shows how work policies can still apply when the conduct is serious enough or poses work health and safety risks. The Arts Centre Melbourne is the country’s biggest performing arts centre known for hosting regular performances from Opera Australia, the Australian Ballet and the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra among others.



After the centre’s Christmas party ended at 7pm in December 2024, some of its employees walked to Beer DeLuxe, a venue on the corner of Flinders and Swanston streets in Melbourne. Related Article Unfair dismissal Woman wins $24k after being fired from ex-husband’s nightclub over explicit photo While standing together in a smoking area at the pub, the officer alleged the venue planner, who he had not met before, was being abusive about other employees, referring to them as “c---s”, which the officer found obnoxious “as a practising Christian”. The officer said he tried to leave the conversation, but that as he was walking away, his colleague followed him and called him a “weak f---ing c---“, making him feel “very unsafe”. The commission noted there was conflicting evidence about whether the venue planner had indeed called the officer a “weak f---ing c---” and that there was insufficient evidence that he had “physically pursued” the officer.



The officer said he pushed the man away, labelling this action as a “clumsy push” or a “shove”. However, commissioner Mark Perica said regardless of how it was described, the blow was “clearly an assault” that caused the man to stumble several metres and fall over a gas heater, risking the venue planner’s safety. The Arts Centre Melbourne spire is a city landmark. Getty Images The officer later admitted that he had also said “well, that’s gay” in response to the venue planner repeatedly saying the word “c---”. Perica, who presided over the case, said the officer’s stated reasons for not mentioning this fact earlier – including that he was “unsure it was something he could discuss” and that “there are issues because of his faith” – did himself no credit. The venue planner said his memory of specific events was “hazy” because of his ADHD and alcohol consumption, but that he could “broadly remember” what had happened, including the officer referring to something – although he couldn’t recall what – in a derogatory manner, as “gay”, which he found offensive as a gay man.



Perica accepted the officer’s allegation that the venue planner had, in response to the statement, “gone off his head” and reacted with verbal aggression, but concluded this did not justify the officer striking him and causing an “obvious and imminent risk of injury”. Perica rejected the officer’s claim that he had acted in self-defence and said that being offended on the basis of faith was not enough to justify a physical reaction. Dismissal was an “entirely proportional” consequence, the commissioner said. And while the venue planner should have been warned for his disrespectful communication, the commissioner said that conduct did not warrant the same consequences. The only direct witness was a senior manager at ACM who said what he saw was “a sloppy, big right-hand punch ... a classic pub punch” delivered by the officer. CCTV footage from the event was lost by the venue, but a manager at Beer DeLuxe gave a general description of the video that showed the altercation. Workplace lawyer Caroline Mense, of Legal Enablers, said the case showed serious misconduct linked to a work function did not necessarily end with the event itself.



Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case “The connection to employment can continue well beyond the venue and the scheduled event finish time,” she said. The officer also attempted to argue his dismissal was harsh because it happened the week before Christmas. The commissioner said while this timing could be harsh “in some circumstances”, the harshness of this fact was “of minimal weight” in this case. Ultimately, Perica said the officer had failed to comply with ACM and Victorian Public Service policies requiring him to treat co-workers with respect, even beyond the workplace. “It is not possible to show a person respect in the process of striking them to the head,” he said. The Arts Centre declined to comment. Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: Sugar City to cricket centrepiece? How Mackay secured a historic Test, and its bold vision of what’s to come
World.content:
Great Barrier Reef Arena in Mackay on the afternoon of the first day during the Test clash between Australia and Bangladesh.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Mackay was grappling with an economic crisis that left the city “at the bottom of the trough”, a group of sporting advocates plotted to transform the region into a cricketing epicentre. While Harrup Park has stood for 78 years, the past decade has been spent building towards a vision: to possess the best arena in regional Queensland capable of bringing international spectacles to the Sugar City. That moment finally arrived when Australia cruised to victory by an innings and 51 runs against Bangladesh inside two sold-out days at the venue’s Great Barrier Reef Arena. When asked from Harrup Park if there was a moment in the city’s history with a comparable buzz, restaurateur Adrian Connors – who has lived in the area for 36 years – replied: “I don’t believe there is.” “Mackay has probably been lacking really big events like this, and I think we’re obviously very capable,” he said. “It’s probably one of the first times we can actually feel the benefit and the energy and the vibe around town. Mitchell Starc and the Australian cricket team celebrate in Mackay. Getty Images



“To see people dressed up in their outfits, Australian jerseys, walking down Nebo Road, Bridge Road, Juliet Street, is just unreal, and it’s put a real atmosphere in town.” A 12-hour drive north of Brisbane and with a population of 130,000, Mackay’s main economic drivers had centred around coal mining and sugar cane. When the price of coal plummeted in the 2010s, a population exodus, business closures and financial upheaval followed. Related Article Test cricket ‘No urgency’: Carey calls on selectors to back Labuschagne after another poor series But sport, according to mayor Greg Williamson, promised opportunity to diversify the economy. “When I first got the job in 2016, we were at the bottom of the trough. Sport is one of the ways, I believe, you can pull a community out of that trough,” he said. Williamson said about $1 million a year was spent to bring sport, business and tourism events to Mackay, with service industries growing their capacity to handle larger-scale spectacles – including NRL semi-finals (2021) and AFLW clashes.



“I’m sure there are a lot of people in Australia saying, ‘Where is Mackay? Why is there a Test match being played in Mackay?’” Williamson said. “That’s the question you need to have people asking because that will lead to people saying they might come. That leads to investment, and that leads to growth. “The pitch is always, can you do it? Yes. Will the grounds stand up to it? Absolutely. Do we have the capacity with the management teams to actually deliver the event? Yes.” Harrup Park’s growth has been the driving force for change. Great Barrier Reef Arena pictured on the morning of day one of the clash between Australia and Bangladesh. Nick Wright Campaigning initiatives spearheaded by the likes of general manager Adrian Young and Mackay Cricket Association president Terry Doolan reaped $20 million between state and government funding commitments for stage one of their Great Barrier Reef Arena vision and brought elite cricket to the region. A 2000-seat grandstand (included in the 10,000 spectator capacity) and broadcast facilities have been built to meet the demands of marquee events.



A further $23.5 million in state funding was secured to begin stage two. Williamson said he and Young have ventured to Canberra pushing for federal support to complete the near $50 million second stage for the multi-sport hub and elite training facility. Ideally, an onsite hotel would be included. The expansions have already accommodated WBBL and one-day international fixtures, with Queensland Cricket chief Terry Svenson stressing it had “been a strategic objective” for a decade to deliver more elite cricket to regional areas. Former Brisbane Heat batter Josie Dooley in action at Harrup Park. AAP “The facilities at Great Barrier Reef Arena are excellent and clearly show the ongoing commitment and investment into the venue that have allowed a Test match to be played,” Svenson said. Connors – who runs Mackay restaurant The Dispensary with his brother Damien – noted a spike in interstate and intrastate visitors from the Tuesday before the Test started, with hospitality trade tripling. Similarly, on day one of the Test a Greek restaurant was booked out until 9pm, with a lamb shortage ensuing. While Connors felt “our connectivity between the experiences outside of cricket needs to improve” to enhance tourism and service sectors, the fact the Test lasted two days provided opportunities for travellers to experience the “areas which are undiscovered, and a lot of people don’t know of”.



Just some of those hotspots include the northern beaches regions – the Eimeo Pacific Hotel perhaps laying claim to one of the greatest pub views in the country – Pioneer Valley rainforests west of town, and the Cape Hillsborough beaches further north. Luke “Sparrow” Gillian has spearheaded Australian Cricket Tours for more than 25 years – bringing with him dozens of followers, and visiting 93 cricket grounds across the world. The view from the Eimeo Pacific Hotel in Mackay’s northern beaches. Nick Wright The Melbourne-based organiser brought at least 20 people to Mackay from all around the country and will bring 256 travellers to October’s three-Test series in South Africa. “Every night after play, wherever we are in the world, we go somewhere different – this rooftop somewhere in India, this beer garden in Cape Town … we’ll always make sure we get out in society and the culture of where we are,” Gillian said. “That’s the beauty of going back to a city year in, year out – you understand where you want to go, and what you did last year.

World.title: Horizon lands gold drilling trifecta in WA Murchison
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Horizon lands gold drilling trifecta in WA Murchison Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor August 25, 2026 — 3:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Horizon Gold has unveiled a trifecta of reverse circulation drilling results across its Gum Creek project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, 100km southeast of Meekatharra, extending mineralisation a whopping 800m south of the existing resource at its Howards prospect. At the same time, the drill bit has been delivering broad and high-grade hits at the company’s Heron South and Melbourne Bitter targets. Horizon is drilling into a serious brownfields growth story. Its 663-square-kilometre gold camp holds 37.97 million tonnes grading 1.89 grams per tonne (g/t) for 2.3 million ounces and has produced more than one million ounces historically. A 48-target exploration runway emerged from an earlier review of ground, peppered by more than 56,000 historical holes totalling over 2400km, with more than 65 per cent of the holes less than 50m deep. Recent reverse circulation drilling at Horizon Gold’s Gum Creek project area in Western Australia’s Murchison region. At Howards, 27km southeast of the historic Gidgee mill, the existing 245,300-ounce resource stretches over 1.3km of strike. Every hole drilled on 100m-spaced lines immediately south of the resource intersected gold, extending known mineralisation a further 800m. Standout results from the recent drilling at Howards included one hole that threw up 6m grading 5.57g/t gold from 70m, including a 3-metre section at 9.91g/t from 71m. A second hole hit 9m at 2.27g/t from 41m, while a third delivered 4m at 4.65g/t from 70m, including a cracking one-metre high-grade core of 17.30g/t gold.



‘The impressive results and follow up drilling have the potential to enhance the Project economics beyond the recent DFS.’ Horizon Gold managing director Scott Williamson Closer to Gidgee, at Heron South 15km south-southeast of the historic mill, the existing 78,900-ounce resource delivered both width and grade. Results were led by 6m at 12.67g/t from 114m, including a spectacular one-metre slice at 58.70g/t, alongside 25m at 1.79g/t from 84m in a second hole and 12m at 2.35g/t gold from 142m depth in a third. In total, nine holes struck thick mineralisation of 2.5g/t or more, with Horizon saying the drilling confirmed continuity and highlighted potential expansion down dip and to the south along strike. North of the proposed Gidgee processing hub, Melbourne Bitter sits 26km from Gidgee and holds 21,300 ounces. Shallow drilling returned 21m at 2.14g/t from just 24m, including 8m at 3.64g/t. Horizon says the results confirmed existing grades and widths, extended mineralisation south and highlighted potential for greater width and grade south and west of existing drilling. The latest results follow impressive drilling at Kingfisher, Hawk and Swan, where the company sees potential resource additions outside the mine plan in the recent definitive feasibility study (DFS). According to management, substantial underground and sulphide resources also remain outside the open-pit study, giving Horizon several potential avenues to build beyond its existing development case. Horizon Gold managing director Scott Williamson said: “The impressive results from Howards, Heron South, and Melbourne Bitter highlight the potential for significant resource expansion across the Gum Creek Project and follow up drilling prior to updating the respective resource estimations have the potential to enhance the Project economics beyond the recent DFS.”



Diamond drilling is continuing at Swan, Kingfisher and Wilsons, while reverse circulation drilling rolls on elsewhere at Gum Creek. At Heron South, Horizon is drilling two diamond holes to unravel the structural controls of high-grade plunging shoots and guide further expansion drilling before its resource is updated. Horizon is also lining up infill drilling at Howards before a resource update later this year, while further shallow drilling will precede Melbourne Bitter’s next resource estimate. The company says the highly prospective southern half of Melbourne Bitter’s prospecting licence has yet to be drilled. Gum Creek sits in heavyweight gold country alongside multi-million-ounce camps such as Wiluna, Meekatharra, Cue, Mt Magnet and Agnew/Lawlers. The project also comes with serious mining muscle already in place, including a 110-person camp, operational airstrip, tailings facilities and haul roads linking 37 historic open pits and three underground mines. For Horizon, any additional resources that ultimately prove economic could slot into a development plan already taking shape. The DFS envisages a central 2.4-million-tonne-per-annum Gidgee plant and 880,000 ounces of recovered gold over 10 years, with a whopping pre-tax net present value of $1.307 billion at a five per cent discount rate. The study forecasts average production of 88,000 ounces a year, peaking at 114,000 ounces in year two and $1.854 billion in pre-tax free cashflow from a 728,000-ounce reserve, based on a A$5500 gold price. It has also pencilled in all-in sustaining costs of A$2995 per ounce and $350M in construction capex.



With gold now trading at US$4668 (A$6550) per ounce, Australian spot prices sit more than A$1000 above the DFS assumption, adding some serious tailwind to Horizon’s resource-growth push. Horizon has already laid the foundations for a major new gold mine at Gum Creek. With three more deposits showing room to grow, fresh resource estimates on the way and the drill bit firing on all six cylinders, the company looks set for a busy period ahead, building a much bigger house on top. World.title: United Dons vow no ‘jumping at shadows’ now that McVeigh has top job
World.content:
In today’s AFL briefing: Dons unveil McVeigh, promise unity

Melbourne’s man of Steele ready for finals return Bombers declare unity after McVeigh wins top job Jon Pierik Essendon president Andrew Welsh insists the Bombers have never been more united and will not “jump at shadows” after a rogue club member declared he was planning to lead a board challenge because James Hird was overlooked for the role as senior coach. Mark McVeigh’s family were on board on Tuesday when he was formally announced as the club’s senior coach. Jason South



The Bombers on Monday confirmed Mark McVeigh, also a former Bomber and one-time teammate of Hird’s, had won the top role. Ahead of McVeigh’s introductory press conference on Tuesday, Brett Crabtree, 33, reportedly reaffirmed his comments on SEN last week, that he was leading a group of members frustrated by the Bombers’ long-time failures and alleged governance issues. Loading However, when contacted by this masthead on Tuesday, Crabtree said the fresh comments reported by SEN and attributed to him on Tuesday were not made by him. Welsh and Bombers chief executive Tim Roberts were strong in their defence of their board, Welsh declaring the club was tired of those who “live in the shadows” and want to destabilise the club.



“You know, year after year, and we get people coming out of the shadows that want to challenge the board. I can tell you, since I’ve been here, this club has never been more united,” Welsh said. “So, these people want to keep living in the shadows and come and try and destabilise our club. We don’t jump at shadows. We’re a strong club, and we’ll continue to make sure that we’re making the right decisions on behalf of our members and our teams and our staff to get this club moving forward again.” Crabtree, a financial planner, last week mooted a possible challenge to the board. SEN reported on Tuesday that challenge was still on, but Crabtree told this masthead he would not provide a “running commentary”. Crabtree last week said only Hird should have been considered for the top job, replacing Brad Scott who departed the club in May.



He said he had never met Hird, the club great and former premiership skipper, whose second stint as coach in 2015 ended amid the fall-out of the supplements’ scandal. Roberts said the Bombers were aware of Crabtree’s long-time agitation, but “we’re just going on doing our thing”. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview “Our members asked us to run a thorough process to find the best candidate, and I think Mark can talk as a candidate as part of that process. But, we’re really comfortable that we’ve done that, and that’s what the overwhelming number of members have told us, and that’s what we’ve done,” Roberts said. “If people want to challenge us around that, then so be it. But we’re really strong where we are. We’re a united club. We just have to look around at the people here. This is a big, strong football club. That’s who we are, and we’ll just move forward as we see best. And we’re united in that. “



Melbourne’s bargain recruit makes finals return Marc McGowan Melbourne midfielder Jack Steele has refused to sink the boots into his old club St Kilda as he prepares to play his first final in three years. Now with Melbourne, Jack Steele will return to the finals on Saturday against Carlton. Photograph by Chris Hopkins Unwanted by Ross Lyon and the Saints – including being used as the starting substitute in a game late last season – Steele accepted a trade to the Demons and has been a key contributor under Steven King.



St Kilda instead loaded up on high-priced recruits, while paying a big chunk of Steele’s remaining contract, but failed to make even the wildcard round as Melbourne exceeded expectations. The Demons handed over only a 2027 third-round selection for Steele, in the same trade period they offloaded Clayton Oliver and Christian Petracca. Jack Steele bolstered Melbourne’s midfield after the departures of Christian Petracca and Clayton Oliver. via Getty Images “It’s been a bit of a whirlwind of a 12 months, to be honest,” Steele said. “Comparison is the thief of joy, as they say, so I don’t really want to compare my position now to where the Saints are at the moment. But I’m really grateful for the opportunity Melbourne have given me.”



Steele credited King for him being a happier, “less grumpy” person, but declined to compare the first-year coach’s style to Lyon’s. Related Article Updated

AFL off-field behaviour Embarrassed Tigers say Mad Monday antics did not reference Swans scandal He said being free of the burdens that come with being a captain was also refreshing, while still serving as a mentor to younger teammates “at my own pace”. The Demons were stiff to finish seventh with 15 wins, particularly because in-form Carlton await them at the MCG on Saturday night. The clash presents another chance for Steele to face-off with Blues champion Patrick Cripps.



“From my first days as a Saint, I played on Patty Cripps a fair bit,” he said. “I was always that match-up, so I assume that’s going to continue to happen this week. He’s a great player, and he’s won two Brownlows for a reason, so it’s going to be a real challenge.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: ‘Who will staff them?’ Dentists slam Labor’s promise of free dental care
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHealthcare ‘Who will staff them?’ Dentists slam Labor’s promise of free dental care Melissa Cunningham August 25, 2026 — 4:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victoria’s dental industry has slammed an election promise by Premier Ben Carroll to establish 10 free public dental clinics, dubbing it a political ploy to buy votes and warning it could blow out years-long waiting lists for the state’s most vulnerable patients. The government announced on Saturday that it would create clinics with capacity to treat more than 100,000 people annually, at a cost of $230 million over three years under an Australian-first proposal, if Labor wins the November state election. Australian Dental Association Victorian branch president Dr Carolyn Ng has warned the proposal would increase waiting times for the more than 2 million low-income or vulnerable people who are eligible for public dental care. Wayne Taylor Carroll vowed anyone would be able to access dental care at the seven Melbourne and three regional walk-in clinics. But the Australian Dental Association’s Victorian branch president, Dr Carolyn Ng, has criticised the proposal, warning it will only increase waiting times for the more than 2 million low-income or vulnerable people who are currently eligible for public dental care and already facing delays of up to three years.



“By opening up the funding, which is only $75 million per year, to everyone in the state, it means that ones who are already identified as being at most risk of dental disease are going to miss out,” the Melbourne dentist and specialist orthodontist said. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare A simple tooth fix emptied Natasha’s super and left her in constant pain “It will only worsen the waitlists for them. The most vulnerable people will miss out on having their teeth saved.” She also questioned how the government was going to staff the new clinics, saying publicly funded dental chairs were already operating at only about 50 per cent capacity around the state due to a workforce crisis plaguing the industry. “How is he [Carroll] going to staff these clinics?” Ng said.



“Will he to be taking them from the public sector, where we already have huge shortages?” Associate Professor Matt Hopcraft, a dental expert from the University of Melbourne, was also critical of the plan. “The whole thing they are proposing just doesn’t make any sense to me,” Hopcraft said. “Fundamentally, it feels like an attempt to buy votes by tapping into a very real public desire for expanded dental funding.” He said thousands of Victorians were increasingly losing teeth or ending up in hospital due to long public dental waiting lists, and $75 million a year and the proposed new clinics would not fix that. “There’s absolutely a huge need for more emergency dental care, but at the state level, the problem that Victoria has is that they’re not staffing their existing clinics,” he said.





Under Labor’s plan, patients would be able to get free check-ups and treatment such as fillings, root canals and extractions. Hopcraft said this proposal abandoned the established public health model of care, which focused on high-need patients, and instead opened access to everyone in a move that would make dental care harder to reach for those with the greatest need. The state government plans to spend $230 million over three years under its proposal. Quentin Jones It is a concern shared by Ng, who fears the government’s proposed walk-in “urgent care” model of clinics would struggle to deliver complex emergency treatment such as root canals because these procedures often require multiple visits. “A single walk-in, walk-out clinic is likely to lead to more extractions, not better care,” she said.



The current wait listing for public dental care is open only to eligible Victorians, such as those with a healthcare card. The government has vowed these existing services, which treat tens of thousands of Victorians a year, will continue under the proposal. Hopcraft said the promise of free dental clinics was uncannily similar to former premier Daniel Andrews’ 2018 pre-election commitment to introduce free dental vans, under a program known as Smile Squad, for all public school students. He estimated eight years on from the Smile Squad pledge that only about 10 per cent of children were getting dental exams through the free vans, and fewer were getting treatment. “That was another policy that also had absolutely no basis,” Hopcraft said. “One of my biggest concerns is they’ve [Labor] got a recent history of promising something really big that sounds amazing on paper, and then failing to deliver on it.” Ng said that while the free vans were meant to improve children’s dental health, all the data suggested tooth decay was on the rise among children in Victoria.



The dental experts said the focus should be on expanding Medicare to cover more dental services at a national level, while the state government should prioritise urgently tackling staffing shortfalls. They warned that publicly funded dentists were paid 30 per cent less in Victoria than the national average, making retention of staff difficult. Editor's pick Exclusive

Melbourne Assembly These suburbs may never be the same as Melbourne’s population soars to 10 million Ng also pointed out 66 towns in Victoria (making up about 13 per cent of the state’s population) still lack fluoridated tap water. She said expanding fluoridation to unfluoridated regional communities would directly prevent severe dental decay and hospitalisations. The Victorian Council of Social Service urged the government to target low-income people first to stop vulnerable families being forced to raid their retirement savings or put up with excruciating pain if the plan went ahead.



The council’s chief executive, Juanita Pope, said more than 10,000 Victorians had already been forced to draw on superannuation savings to meet urgent dental needs. “We’d love to see universal free dental care, but until that is a reality we need to focus on Victorians who are struggling to put food on the table and pay the rent,” Pope said. The government as said urgent patients would be given priority at the clinics and details about the workforce and proposed locations would be released in the coming weeks. “I’m fighting for the tens of thousands of working people who can’t afford to see a dentist,” the premier said in a statement. “It’s structural cost-of-living support, and it’s a national first.” The government has been contacted for comment. World.title: Hundreds of buyers in limbo as major Sydney developer Bathla Group collapses
World.content:
NationalNSWInsolvency Hundreds of buyers in limbo as major Sydney developer Bathla Group collapses Ellie Busby and Anthony Segaert Updated August 25, 2026 — 4:25pm ,first published 10:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of apartment buyers have been left in limbo over the collapse of a major Australian developer, further derailing the NSW government’s ambitions for hundreds of thousands of new homes. Bathla Group entered voluntary administration on Tuesday and corporate restructuring agency Teneo was appointed to oversee the company and its hundreds of related entities, including Universal Property Group and Raj & Jai Construction. Bathla Group has collapsed. Louie Douvis The collapse of the group, which last week boasted of 3500 homes, apartments or subdivision lots being under construction, will be felt the hardest in north- and south-western Sydney, which has been reshaped by the developer’s prolific greenfield builds. The collapse has left buyers who purchased off the plan in limbo, after major developments in Box Hill and Castle Hill were plagued by delays. Work on some western Sydney Bathla projects stalled in recent months, with tradesmen walking off sites and some claiming they had not been paid.



Bathla, which has built more than 15,000 homes since 1997, has expanded into regional NSW, Victoria and South Australia. Its collapse adds further pressure to the state government’s housing agenda, already struggling amid concerns about the feasibility of apartment construction west of Parramatta. Developers have warned for more than a year that rising construction and material costs, combined with high government taxes and sluggish growth in the west of the city, were making the development of new homes unviable. Bathla founder and director Bhart Bhushan said the “orderly restructure of business” was due to “a perfect storm” of declining sales, rising construction costs and the federal government’s budget. “Our first thoughts are with our employees and the customers who have put their faith in us to deliver their dream of home ownership,” he said in a post on social media. “It is my sincere hope this process can allow that to happen by working collaboratively with the administrators, our suppliers, contractors and lending partners.”



Bathla has faced significant financial problems for the past year: it had more than $3 billion in debt and was in the sights of the state’s building regulator, which had inspected its properties more than 40 times over recent months. Related Article Exclusive

City life Janice was thrilled to buy her own unit. But she has no idea if she will ever move in Building Commission NSW last week issued its associated entity, Raj & Jai Construction, and its director two fines worth $54,000 over improper conduct in working on two Schofields properties without the required insurance. Bathla chief executive Robert Loader said in a statement the company recognised it was a “difficult situation” and the appointment of administrators was “in the best interest of all stakeholders”. “The business has been through a period of declining sales and falling property prices, while construction costs have increased,” he said. “We will work constructively with the administrators to support the continued delivery of much-needed housing for western Sydney.”



Industry sources said Bathla had about 43 lenders, none of which were major banks, making it reliant on private credit. That sector has been subject to intense regulatory and commercial scrutiny after it surged into areas that banks vacated following the global financial crisis, lured by the prospect of charging riskier clients high interest rates for loans. But this year several major private credit funds have had to pause or limit withdrawals from their own financial backers amid fears the companies they had loaned money to were at risk of failing to make repayments. Marie Sinclair (left) with her mother, Sue Mancuso, and Janice Cahill, who all purchased off-the-plan units at Bathla Group’s Kembla Grange property. Wolter Peeters “The concentration of Australia’s private credit market in higher-risk real estate construction and development is where we see the greatest area for improvement for investor protection and market integrity,” warned two experts commissioned to write a report on the area last year for the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. In Box Hill, a greenfield suburb on Sydney’s north-western fringe, a $19 million apartment block was due to be built by December 2024, but buyers who had purchased units off the plan in 2022 were still waiting for it to be finished.



In Castle Hill, a major apartment development languished as an abandoned partly flooded hole in the ground, which a spokesperson said was due to delays in getting a “further staged construction certificate” for the site. Further south, in the Illawarra suburb of Kembla Grange, Building Commission NSW identified defects in a series of under-construction units which were meant to be finished by December 2025. That extension date had been extended four times, and a Bathla spokesperson last week said the project was expected to be completed by October or November. Janice Cahill, who bought an apartment at the development off the plan, said last week the delays had affected her mental health. On Tuesday morning she called her real estate agent, asking what the collapse meant, and was assured the project was continuing. Marie Sinclair, whose elderly parents bought an apartment in the same building, visited the site in September and found doors with keys left unattended, graffitied walls, half-finished copper piping and multiple broken surfaces.



A NSW government spokesperson said it would work with Bathla’s administrators to understand the implications of the appointment. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: This shrimp po’ boy is the perfect Brisbane sandwich. Here’s why
World.content:
Eating outFood This shrimp po’ boy is the perfect Brisbane sandwich. Here’s why Don’t know what a po’ boy is? You need to get across it, then eat one ASAP. There’s a catch, though. Matt Shea August 25, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It started with a music video. Before he made sausages and taught barbecue and had kids, Steve Lind was a DJ. Not your ex-boyfriend-with-a-busted-CDJ-DJ – an actual touring DJ with singles and remixes and the rest of it. Steve Lind from Lindy’s Po Boys. Markus Ravik In 2016, Lind found himself in New Orleans. “This was when I was doing a lot of music. I went to LA and did some studio sessions and stuff like that,” he says.



“I had a guest vocalist [Fly Boi Keno] for a song and I wanted to do a music video in New Orleans. I think I spent about two weeks in each city. Real shoestring-budget stuff. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up “I knew nothing about New Orleans – maybe Bourbon Street and that was it. The videographer picked me up from the airport and took me to Parkway Tavern and Bakery. “That’s where I had my first po’ boy. I was like, ‘What the hell is this?’” What the hell is a po’ boy? Originating in New Orleans in 1929 as a cheap (or free) meal for striking streetcar workers, a po’ boy is similar to a submarine sandwich but defined by a more French-leaning roll, which is similar to a traditional baguette but lighter and fluffier inside.



Typical fillings are prawns (shrimp, of course, in US parlance), roast beef and Louisiana hot sausage, and a traditional sandwich might be dressed with lettuce, tomato, pickles and mayonnaise. Similar to a sub but with a more French-leaning baguette: Steve Lind’s shrimp po’ boy. Markus Ravik It’s a relatively simple sanger that was intended as a hearty, affordable stomach filler for those “poor boy” striking streetcar workers. So, what makes it so great? “It’s the simplicity of it,” Lind says. “You can even have them undressed, and a good one will be delicious. A po’ boy is like a good cheeseburger, where all the ingredients hold up and it’s balanced, not boring. But that means you have to take good care with your ingredients.” Lindy’s Po Boys



After that initial trip, Lind returned to New Orleans twice – the second time, in early 2025, specifically to research po’ boys. He then set about trying to recreate them in Brisbane. A year later, Lindy’s Po Boys was born. This column caught it on its third pop-up at Camp Hill Bowls Club earlier this month. On the menu was a pork sausage po’ boy – Lind also operates Big Bad Smallgoods, a specialty sausage company – and a shrimp po’ boy. It’s the latter we think you need to eat ASAP. Lind’s prawns are battered in a combination of plain flour, corn starch and cornflour. Markus Ravik The shrimp po’ boy



It’s been a while since I demolished a sandwich this fast. And that’s maybe because Lind has made something that’s as easy to eat as it is delicious. Let’s start with the bread. It’s made to Lind’s specs by Norman Park’s Golden K Bakery, and it’s crisp on the outside (without being banh mi crunchy) and soft and pillowy on the inside. It’s tasty, textural, moreish. “We used to toast our bread, but that of course adds a bit of time,” Lind says. “This loaf doesn’t need toasting, and it holds up well to the wrap. Every po’ boy I’ve ever had was wrapped, and once you put the hot shrimp or sausage in there, it steams the bread a little, making it softer. That’s really important.” There’s a little bit going on with the dressing. Lind uses a moderate amount of iceberg lettuce, a few slices of tomato, and Fehlbergs burger pickles. He then gives each bun a squirt of Hellmann’s mayonnaise, Heinz tomato sauce, and Louisiana Hot Sauce for “acidity and sweetness”. Each bun gets a squirt of Hellmann’s mayonnaise, Heinz tomato sauce and Louisiana Hot Sauce. Markus Ravik



For prawns, there’s nothing fancy, with Lind opting for wild-caught prawns from the supermarket, which still have a bit of flavour but their price enables him to really pile them into the roll, just as they do in New Orleans. What he has really leaned into is his prawn batter. “I talked to Ben [Kirk] from [burger restaurant] Mr Jeebus and he gave me a whole bunch of things to think about,” Lind says. “Like, if I add sugar to my batter, it’s going to make it softer, and anything with starch will make it crispier.” Lind wanted to keep it super crispy and eventually landed on a combination of plain flour, corn starch, and cornflour, for a dash of extra colour. Prepare to become a po’ boy nerd



Lind describes himself as a po’ boy nerd (to be fair, he’s constantly on social media resharing sandwich content from New Orleans), and his local recreation will likely make you a believer too. Is this the perfect sandwich? Markus Ravik In a sense, it’s the perfect sandwich – at least in terms of what we sandwich fans look for. It’s got all that texture from the fried prawns (which remain juicy inside), crispy iceberg, and precision baked bread, but then stacks of acid, and salt and sweetness from the dressings and sauces. Also, unlike a banh mi or other baguette-based sandwiches, it’s a cinch to eat. I ate one alongside the sausage po’ boy and still wanted another. Not because I was hungry, really, but because I wanted to keep the sensation rolling. But also maybe because this is the last time I’ll get to eat one for a month or two. Lindy’s Po Boys is a semi-regular pop-up, so Lind isn’t entirely sure when the next will be, although he’s currently aiming for the King’s Birthday long weekend in early October.



We want you to eat this sandwich so we’ll keep you posted. Where to get it The Lindy’s Po Boy shrimp po’ boy is $22. The pop-up typically appears at Camp Hill Bowls Club, 150 Ferguson Road, Camp Hill.

World.title: Embarrassed Tigers say Mad Monday antics did not reference Swans scandal
World.content:
Updated SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Embarrassed Tigers say Mad Monday antics did not reference Swans scandal Sam McClure Updated August 25, 2026 — 4:02pm ,first published August 25, 2026 — 9:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Richmond players seen striking each other with belts in footage taken during Mad Monday celebrations have expressed embarrassment about their behaviour but denied they were mocking the scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans. The Tigers released a statement on Tuesday afternoon in which they said they had questioned the players about their conduct at the Garfield Hotel in Gippsland on Monday. “Richmond is aware of a video circulating from a player end of season gathering,” the statement said. “The club has spoken to the players who have expressed their embarrassment over their behaviour.



“The players are adamant they were in no way referencing or making light of recent matters.” In one piece of vision of the Tigers’ celebration, young midfielder Josh Smillie appears to pull down his pants and feign shock as he is repeatedly struck on the backside by a teammate. A scene from Richmond’s celebrations at the Garfield Hotel. MEDIA-MODE.COM He appears to be spanked three times in the video and then after a fourth slap, reacts differently. Another Mad Monday clip shows Richmond midfielder Tim Taranto using a belt to strike a shirtless teammate. The footage emerged just a week after five Sydney players were suspended for the remainder of the season for breaches of club standards during a night of partying that ended in a hotel room at the Pullman East Melbourne.



Allegations published by the Herald Sun included that one woman, who was also in the room, had claimed she was slapped on the buttocks four times instead of the three slaps that had been agreed. Richmond players celebrate Mad Monday. MEDIA-MODE.COM Five Sydney players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon – have been suspended for breaching club standards, and a separate police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault at a Melbourne hotel continues. No charges have been laid and this masthead is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the suspended Swans players. The Richmond players told the club their antics were not related to the Swans scandal at all. Richmond players outside the venue in Garfield. MEDIA-MODE.COM



Photos taken of Richmond players at the post-season celebration on Monday appear to show pints of beer lined up on a ledge, a player climbing on a teammate’s shoulders and reaching onto a roof covering, and two players outside the venue appearing to urinate against a fence. The AFL has been contacted for comment on the Mad Monday celebration. A statement was released on the Garfield Hotel’s social media accounts defending the players. “We hosted the Richmond Football Club at our venue today, and we could not speak more highly of the way they conducted themselves. For such a young group, they were extremely respectful and a fun group of boys to deal with,” the statement read.



“They enjoyed a few quiet beers to unwind after a long season, and we see nothing wrong with that. They had booked out the venue for the afternoon, so they were the only patrons on site. They enjoyed their afternoon and moved on. “In our view, this has been blown out of proportion. Two members of the media were waiting on their arrival this morning and remained on site filming in the hope of capturing a misstep, which we consider disappointing.” The footage of the Tigers prompted federal Labor MP Dan Repacholi to criticise the behaviour. “Right now we need good blokes out there having the conversations around this and calling this out for what it is because this is unacceptable, and we need to make sure we do better,” he said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 The tough questions Hird fielded during his Essendon coaching interview The Tigers’ season finished on Saturday after their loss to Geelong. On Monday, AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon delivered a strongly worded statement at the league’s finals launch. As the Swans crisis continues, Dillon said respect for women was not negotiable. There have been several incidents over the past few years at Mad Monday celebrations – the day to mark a club’s end of season – that have sparked controversy about player behaviour.

World.title: ‘Classic pub punch’ costs man his job after trading slurs with colleague
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal ‘Classic pub punch’ costs man his job after trading slurs with colleague Millie Muroi August 25, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Melbourne man who punched a colleague and told him his swearing about other work colleagues was “gay” after a work Christmas party has failed to regain his job after the workplace umpire ruled his sacking was valid. The Fair Work Commission found on Monday that the building maintenance officer, who had worked for the Arts Centre Melbourne since January 2020, struck a colleague – the head of venue planning – at a pub after the Christmas party in 2024. The incident occurred after a work Christmas party. Getty Images While employers generally have limited right to control employees’ behaviour outside work hours, Monday’s decision shows how work policies can still apply when the conduct is serious enough or poses work health and safety risks. The Arts Centre Melbourne is the country’s biggest performing arts centre known for hosting regular performances from Opera Australia, the Australian Ballet and the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra among others.



After the centre’s Christmas party ended at 7pm in December 2024, some of its employees walked to Beer DeLuxe, a venue on the corner of Flinders and Swanston streets in Melbourne. Related Article Unfair dismissal Woman wins $24k after being fired from ex-husband’s nightclub over explicit photo While standing together in a smoking area at the pub, the officer alleged the venue planner, who he had not met before, was being abusive about other employees, referring to them as “c---s”, which the officer found obnoxious “as a practising Christian”. The officer said he tried to leave the conversation, but that as he was walking away, his colleague followed him and called him a “weak f---ing c---“, making him feel “very unsafe”. The commission noted there was conflicting evidence about whether the venue planner had indeed called the officer a “weak f---ing c---” and that there was insufficient evidence that he had “physically pursued” the officer.



The officer said he pushed the man away, labelling this action as a “clumsy push” or a “shove”. However, commissioner Mark Perica said regardless of how it was described, the blow was “clearly an assault” that caused the man to stumble several metres and fall over a gas heater, risking the venue planner’s safety. The Arts Centre Melbourne spire is a city landmark. Getty Images The officer later admitted that he had also said “well, that’s gay” in response to the venue planner repeatedly saying the word “c---”. Perica, who presided over the case, said the officer’s stated reasons for not mentioning this fact earlier – including that he was “unsure it was something he could discuss” and that “there are issues because of his faith” – did himself no credit. The venue planner said his memory of specific events was “hazy” because of his ADHD and alcohol consumption, but that he could “broadly remember” what had happened, including the officer referring to something – although he couldn’t recall what – in a derogatory manner, as “gay”, which he found offensive as a gay man.



Perica accepted the officer’s allegation that the venue planner had, in response to the statement, “gone off his head” and reacted with verbal aggression, but concluded this did not justify the officer striking him and causing an “obvious and imminent risk of injury”. Perica rejected the officer’s claim that he had acted in self-defence and said that being offended on the basis of faith was not enough to justify a physical reaction. Dismissal was an “entirely proportional” consequence, the commissioner said. And while the venue planner should have been warned for his disrespectful communication, the commissioner said that conduct did not warrant the same consequences. The only direct witness was a senior manager at ACM who said what he saw was “a sloppy, big right-hand punch ... a classic pub punch” delivered by the officer. CCTV footage from the event was lost by the venue, but a manager at Beer DeLuxe gave a general description of the video that showed the altercation. Workplace lawyer Caroline Mense, of Legal Enablers, said the case showed serious misconduct linked to a work function did not necessarily end with the event itself.



Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case “The connection to employment can continue well beyond the venue and the scheduled event finish time,” she said. The officer also attempted to argue his dismissal was harsh because it happened the week before Christmas. The commissioner said while this timing could be harsh “in some circumstances”, the harshness of this fact was “of minimal weight” in this case. Ultimately, Perica said the officer had failed to comply with ACM and Victorian Public Service policies requiring him to treat co-workers with respect, even beyond the workplace. “It is not possible to show a person respect in the process of striking them to the head,” he said. The Arts Centre declined to comment. Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: Sugar City to cricket centrepiece? How Mackay secured a historic Test, and its bold vision of what’s to come
World.content:
Great Barrier Reef Arena in Mackay on the afternoon of the first day during the Test clash between Australia and Bangladesh.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Mackay was grappling with an economic crisis that left the city “at the bottom of the trough”, a group of sporting advocates plotted to transform the region into a cricketing epicentre. While Harrup Park has stood for 78 years, the past decade has been spent building towards a vision: to possess the best arena in regional Queensland capable of bringing international spectacles to the Sugar City. That moment finally arrived when Australia cruised to victory by an innings and 51 runs against Bangladesh inside two sold-out days at the venue’s Great Barrier Reef Arena. When asked from Harrup Park if there was a moment in the city’s history with a comparable buzz, restaurateur Adrian Connors – who has lived in the area for 36 years – replied: “I don’t believe there is.” “Mackay has probably been lacking really big events like this, and I think we’re obviously very capable,” he said. “It’s probably one of the first times we can actually feel the benefit and the energy and the vibe around town. Mitchell Starc and the Australian cricket team celebrate in Mackay. Getty Images



“To see people dressed up in their outfits, Australian jerseys, walking down Nebo Road, Bridge Road, Juliet Street, is just unreal, and it’s put a real atmosphere in town.” A 12-hour drive north of Brisbane and with a population of 130,000, Mackay’s main economic drivers had centred around coal mining and sugar cane. When the price of coal plummeted in the 2010s, a population exodus, business closures and financial upheaval followed. Related Article Test cricket ‘No urgency’: Carey calls on selectors to back Labuschagne after another poor series But sport, according to mayor Greg Williamson, promised opportunity to diversify the economy. “When I first got the job in 2016, we were at the bottom of the trough. Sport is one of the ways, I believe, you can pull a community out of that trough,” he said. Williamson said about $1 million a year was spent to bring sport, business and tourism events to Mackay, with service industries growing their capacity to handle larger-scale spectacles – including NRL semi-finals (2021) and AFLW clashes.



“I’m sure there are a lot of people in Australia saying, ‘Where is Mackay? Why is there a Test match being played in Mackay?’” Williamson said. “That’s the question you need to have people asking because that will lead to people saying they might come. That leads to investment, and that leads to growth. “The pitch is always, can you do it? Yes. Will the grounds stand up to it? Absolutely. Do we have the capacity with the management teams to actually deliver the event? Yes.” Harrup Park’s growth has been the driving force for change. Great Barrier Reef Arena pictured on the morning of day one of the clash between Australia and Bangladesh. Nick Wright Campaigning initiatives spearheaded by the likes of general manager Adrian Young and Mackay Cricket Association president Terry Doolan reaped $20 million between state and government funding commitments for stage one of their Great Barrier Reef Arena vision and brought elite cricket to the region. A 2000-seat grandstand (included in the 10,000 spectator capacity) and broadcast facilities have been built to meet the demands of marquee events.



A further $23.5 million in state funding was secured to begin stage two. Williamson said he and Young have ventured to Canberra pushing for federal support to complete the near $50 million second stage for the multi-sport hub and elite training facility. Ideally, an onsite hotel would be included. The expansions have already accommodated WBBL and one-day international fixtures, with Queensland Cricket chief Terry Svenson stressing it had “been a strategic objective” for a decade to deliver more elite cricket to regional areas. Former Brisbane Heat batter Josie Dooley in action at Harrup Park. AAP “The facilities at Great Barrier Reef Arena are excellent and clearly show the ongoing commitment and investment into the venue that have allowed a Test match to be played,” Svenson said. Connors – who runs Mackay restaurant The Dispensary with his brother Damien – noted a spike in interstate and intrastate visitors from the Tuesday before the Test started, with hospitality trade tripling. Similarly, on day one of the Test a Greek restaurant was booked out until 9pm, with a lamb shortage ensuing. While Connors felt “our connectivity between the experiences outside of cricket needs to improve” to enhance tourism and service sectors, the fact the Test lasted two days provided opportunities for travellers to experience the “areas which are undiscovered, and a lot of people don’t know of”.



Just some of those hotspots include the northern beaches regions – the Eimeo Pacific Hotel perhaps laying claim to one of the greatest pub views in the country – Pioneer Valley rainforests west of town, and the Cape Hillsborough beaches further north. Luke “Sparrow” Gillian has spearheaded Australian Cricket Tours for more than 25 years – bringing with him dozens of followers, and visiting 93 cricket grounds across the world. The view from the Eimeo Pacific Hotel in Mackay’s northern beaches. Nick Wright The Melbourne-based organiser brought at least 20 people to Mackay from all around the country and will bring 256 travellers to October’s three-Test series in South Africa. “Every night after play, wherever we are in the world, we go somewhere different – this rooftop somewhere in India, this beer garden in Cape Town … we’ll always make sure we get out in society and the culture of where we are,” Gillian said. “That’s the beauty of going back to a city year in, year out – you understand where you want to go, and what you did last year.

World.title: Worst property managers named and shamed in new report
World.content:
Property managers renting out mouldiest, dampest homes Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Big players like Bayleys and Quinovic are named in a new report as the property managers with the mouldiest, coldest and dampest homes.

Findings of the Aotearoa Renters Survey, co-authored by Renters United and Action Station, are igniting calls for firmer regulation of property managers.

But most realtors told RNZ they actually agreed with stricter regulation - stricter than the "light-touch" approach the government has proposed.

The report said more than 40 percent of people who were told their homes met Healthy Homes standards still experienced issues with mould, dampness, or drafts.

A Healthy Homes advisor on the Kāpiti Coast, Jessica Keltie, said she had seen property managers let "quite revolting" home issues slide.

"I know somebody who is a single mum with three high-needs children... Her house, the bathroom literally folded up around her because it was so damp and disgusting."

The report found more than half of those living in Bayleys, Quinovic, Barfoot & Thompson and Crockers homes had experienced issues with mould, coldness and draughts. Of the more than 3000 renters who took the survey, about 500 named their property manager.

In Keltie's experience, many agents were unaware of their obligations under the Healthy Homes standards and Residential Tenancies Act.

She was one of many advocates calling for property managers to be regulated, as well as an independent system for Healthy Homes certification.

The report proposed creating a rental warrant of fitness, awarded from an accredited source.

In March, the government announced proposals to develop a "light touch" approach to regulate property managers, including a register and separate disciplinary tribunal.

The proposed bill - which is still in the drafting stage - would not change realtors' and landlords' ability to self-certify for Healthy Homes.

President of Renters United, Luke Somervell, said property managers were "rogue operators".

"There's no regulation. There's no register. There's no oversight or any ways to pull property managers up for dodgy practices."

The report also recommended a Healthy Homes hotline, where renters could call up when they believed their home was not up to standard.

"If we can raise the bar, then the people who are doing the right thing will benefit," Somervell said. "And the people who are the crooks and the cowboys, they will get pushed out of the market."

With laws like no-cause evictions starting, Somervell said it was renters' turn for legislation that gave them power.

Of the respondents, 25 percent said they had experienced discrimination from a landlord or property manager, often focused on family status or beneficiaries.

"Renters are feeling scared. They feel that the power balance is totally tipped in favour of landlords and property managers," Somervell said.

RNZ approached all 10 realtors mentioned in the report, and a majority said they would support regulation in some form.

Quinovic chief executive Parrish Wong said he was disappointed to see the findings about his company, which ranked second-worst behind Bayleys.

"We take any suggestion that a property managed by Quinovic may not be compliant seriously."

A room in a Wellington rental property advertised by Quinovic for $200 in 2022. Vic deals / Facebook

Quinovic was one of multiple companies that already used an independent Healthy Homes certifier, which Wong said should be enforced.

"We're not experts, we're not builders, we look after properties. So you want to get an expert in there.

"Clear standards and accountability across the sector are good for tenants, property owners, private landlords and professional property managers."

Multiple realtors said they cut ties with landlords who refused to meet standards when the final Healthy Home deadline came into effect last year.

Property Brokers was one of them, saying it scrapped the management of 168 properties where owners were not willing to do the work needed.

A spokesperson said Property Brokers would want to see regulation focused on the performance of a property, rather than simply complying with a checklist.

The spokesperson said the standards of Healthy Homes can be open to interpretation. Instead, they'd like to see policy move towards a property performance model.

The United Kingdom introduced something similar, called Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs), where homes are assessed on measurable performance outcomes rather than solely on prescribed criteria.

Companies like Ray White and Harcourts said they invested in extra education for property managers, in light of a lack of regulation.

Several businesses said they were members of the Real Estate Institute of New Zealand (REINZ), which had advocated for higher professional standards and regulation.

The proposed bill would require property managers and/organisations to be publicly registered, and meet minimum standards of things like education and conduct.

Tama Potaka. Alyse Wright

It would also establish a formal complaints and disciplinary process, and require client funds be held separately from operational funds.

This wasn't the first time legislation has tried to pass on the topic, with a complete scrapping of a similar bill in 2024.

The bill was still being drafted, and would not be finished before the end of this government's term. It will likely be up to the next government to make a change.

"These changes have been informed by discussions with landlords and tenant advocates, and industry bodies for the sector, and this feedback has helped shape a balanced approach that responds to sector needs while keeping regulatory costs low," Associate Minister of Housing Tama Potaka said.

However, private landlords would not need to register under the bill. Both advocates and some realtors disagreed with this, saying that all landlords should be included in the regulation.

Potaka said landlords were already regulated under the Residential Tenancies Act 1986.

World.title: Youths on proposed social media ban: Cautious approval, but questions around enforcement
World.content:
Young people question proposed social media ban Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

"How are you going to enforce this?" That's the response from young people who grew up with social media to the proposed ban for under-16s.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said social media is exposing young people to harmful content, addictive technology and pressure they aren't equipped to deal with, and the government would push ahead with the Online Safety Bill.

"We would never knowingly let our children wander into places in the real world we know to be unsafe. We put boundaries around cars, around alcohol, around gambling, because we know children aren't yet equipped for them."

So, it has been proposed that social media platforms will risk financial penalties if they don't take steps to verify the age of users.

But some Auckland 17- and 18-year-olds say they're not convinced a complete ban will work.

For some teens who jumped on to social media around 12 years old, some of what the government mentioned during their announcement resembled their experiences.

Checkpoint spoke with some Year 13 students from Auckland's Albany Senior High School.

Jeremy Ouwejan said he often saw content that came from online communities such as the manosphere.

"Andrew Tate speaking to young impressionable men about very damaging ideologies like misogyny, transphobia and homophobia, or, armchair psychology that says how to manipulate your friends and how to do certain things.

Andrew Tate. AFP / DANIEL MIHAILESCU

"Or people will say, 'I used to be a dietitian, here's what you should and shouldn't eat.' [Instagram] Reels on working out and harmful gym content saying, 'If you're not benching 100kg are you even a real person?'"

Ouwejan said he also had seen posts that were violent.

"I'll hop onto Reels and I'll be flashed with a [dead] body. It'll completely ruin the experience of just wanting to talk to a friend."

Last year, research from Te Mana Whakaatu / The Classification Office, found young people don't generally go looking for objectionable content. But it could be hard to avoid when it came up on social media, in group chats or was shown around in person.

Some examples of this included pornography and real-world violence.

Another student, Natalie Osmond, told Checkpoint coming across extreme, violent and misogynistic content every day took a toll.

"When you're giving people ranked numerical scores, especially women… it's objectification to the highest level. You can't just put a number value on someone, it's bad it comes with the podcasts.

"A lot of my feed is about Ariana Grande for example, and other female artists. The [comments] will be all about body image and they're just saying horrible things."

Ariana Grande. CHRIS DELMAS

But, she said, social media also came with its positives.

"Social media is also a good way to get informed from people. There's a fine line between getting informed and seeing all of the bad stuff.

"I do think it's a crazy time to be alive and we can see what's going on in any corner of the world."

Osmond agreed restricting some parts of social media and having consequences for creating or promoting harmful content was a good thing.

"I wish it was socially acceptable to have a Nokia brick - I know I could actually do that, but I really couldn't.

"Also, even as a child I remember being 12 years old and it would socially stunt you even if you weren't allowed social media... you're pressured to have it from a very young age."

But Osmond and the other students Checkpoint spoke to weren't convinced a ban would work, with reports from Australia of teens using loopholes to get around it.

Ouwejan said change was needed, but had to be thought through.

"I think currently there is a lot of very young people on some very damaging platforms, and it is changing them for the worse for the rest of their lives.

"However, as we have seen from Australia and what we can interpolate from other studies and other bans, banning is not the way to go - we need a controlled method, but balancing that with free speech."

Another student, Isabella Green, said she was concerned around how the government would enforce a ban.

"How are you going to track and enforce this? That doesn't feel like it's something that would respect the privacy of people."

ACT and New Zealand First will not support the bill, meaning National will need Labour's support if it's to progress.

Not enough evidence - commissioner

Doubts over whether social media ban is enforceable Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle told Checkpoint more evidence into the effectiveness of a complete ban was needed before implementing one in Aotearoa.

"We know that [kids have told] us that they want the internet to be made safer or online harm to be reduced for them. Whether the solution is just in a complete ban, that remains to be seen, and we need to look at the evidence around that."

Children's Commissioner Jane Searle. Stephen Barker / Barker Photography via Child Matters

Searle said that a more comprehensive plan to tackle the issues around social media was needed, rather than just an outright ban.

"I think that we need good education for young people and their families to be able to make good decisions that keep them safe. But we also need to be able to hold tech companies to account and have robust obligations on them.

"Then we need to look at the regulation - do we have an independent regulator?"

She said there was also a concern over young people who may be marginalised or isolated as the result of a ban.

"We need to be very careful when we move forward, and we need to look at the evidence. We need to know, what will this ban look like in practice? How will it actually impact the way that young people are engaging with social media?"

Searle said there wasn't currently enough information to know if a ban would be successful.

"Even if you look at other countries, what they've implemented, it wasn't long ago, so we don't have that evidence to know."

She said more onus needed to be put on social media companies to manage what content they were showing to young people.

"It's about how they design the algorithms, how they engage with young people, how they put checks in places on what age and what is age appropriate."

However, she acknowledged that enforcing regulations on large tech companies would be difficult.

"I think we need to try and we need to put as much in place as possible. And then hopefully we can work with other governments around the world to actually have some influence as well."

World.title: Name suppression sought for man facing historical sexual offending charges
World.content:
A man at the centre of a police investigation into alleged historical sexual offending had "considerable involvement with a great deal of young people," the Crown says.

Police investigating the case are set to make inquiries into the man's relationships with a "significant number of people," a court heard.

The 63-year-old's case was called in the Christchurch District Court on Tuesday before Judge Michael Crosbie. The man's appearance in court was excused.

The man faces five charges of unlawful sexual connection with a boy aged 12-16 and three charges of indecent assault on a boy aged between 12-16. The charges relate to three complainants and date between 1996 to 2005.

The man's lawyer Ethan Huda said on Tuesday that the man was seeking name suppression on the ground that publication of his name would give risk to a fair trial.

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Huda said there were two unique features of the case. This included that police would be approaching some people with what he referred to as a "scripted questionnaire" to "elicit" information from them.

He said police would identify the defendant to the people spoken to as part of their approach.

"Police believe without identifying [the man] they cannot carry out the questionnaire in the way they would like to."

Huda submitted the man's name should not be published until police had finished administering the questionnaire.

He also wanted to know what the questionnaire would say.

In response, Crown prosecutor Courtney Martyn spoke of the approach that police were using as part of their investigation and what groups of people police would approach.

Martyn said the defendant had "considerable involvement with a great deal of young people…"

"The police aren't going around recruiting complainants or recruiting potential complaints," Martyn said.

She said at no stage would the police be trying to elicit complaints.

"What they're going to be saying is police are conducting an investigation into [the defendant] and as part of that investigation we are speaking to people who may have had contact with him and we understand you're one of those people."

Police would not be discussing any further details or specific allegations.

Judge Crosbie reserved his decision.

Detective Inspector Scott Anderson earlier said police would "continue to investigate whether there are other victims, however as the matter is before the courts and there are suppression orders no further comment will be made".

RNZ understands the defendant has lived in Auckland and Christchurch.

Oranga Tamariki deputy chief executive Thomas Ronan earlier told RNZ the agency had been made aware by police that they were investigating allegations of historical offending by a 63-year-old man.

World.title: Wellington City Council executive faces questions from parents of drowned man
World.content:
The father of a man who drowned in Wellington Harbour has compared the response to waterfront risk to that of landslides on Mauao.

A scathing report into the deadly landslide at Mount Maunganui found Tauranga City Council did not act on multiple reports of the risk for more than 20 years.

The comparison by Charles Levings was made at the coroner's inquest into the death of his son, Isaac Levings.

The Christchurch teacher drowned on the waterfront following a concert by the pop band The 1975, three years ago.

Since 2017, six people have drowned in Wellington harbour.

Charles Levings said the inquiry into the Mauao landslide made it clear Tauranga's council ignored advice and recommendations about the risk for decades.

He said Wellington's council had likewise received numerous reports about the risk of drowning on the waterfront, and pointed to a recent review from Water Safety New Zealand that identified it as a high-risk public space.

"It compared the drownings in Auckland waterfront to the drownings in Wellington. Since 2017, when Auckland erected balustrades around their waterfront, there had been no further drownings.

"There have been, up to this date, six tragic and preventable drownings... in Wellington."

During the coronial inquest on Tuesday, Charles Levings put to Wellington City Council chief operating officer, James Roberts, that his council was in a similar situation to Tauranga's.

"They've received a number of reports, recommendations, and advice to make the waterfront... safer, but very little has been done."

James Roberts. Mary Argue / RNZ

Charles Levings acknowledged the work undertaken to improve lighting around the harbour wharf, but said it didn't go far enough.

In response, Roberts told the court the council was well-aware of the risk. He said councillors had been advised of all the relevant recommendations and reports, and the case had been made to install waterfront balustrades in high-risk areas.

In August last year, councillors voted down the recommendation.

In further questioning of Roberts, Charles Levings expressed concern that safety barriers on the waterfront were only seen as protection for "drunk people". It followed evidence presented at the inquest earlier this month about Isaac Levings' level of intoxication on the night he died.

Charles Levings. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Charles Levings told the court he understood opposition to waterfront barriers was strong.

"I know what the council are up against in terms of keyboard warriors. You've got plenty of them who are great advocates of getting rid of all the fences and all the balustrades," he said.

"I just worry that it's being promoted as a barrier for drunk people, but in actual fact, it's a barrier for all people."

He said falling into the harbour was an accident waiting to happen and suggested the council take a different approach - promoting balustrades as part of a larger development plan to make Wellington's waterfront "one of the best" in the country.

"I think you'd get a lot of buy-in from people," he said.

"You may be right," Roberts replied.

During her questioning of Roberts, Margaret Levings, Isaac Levings' mother, queried whether the council fully understood the risk the waterfront presented - citing a police officer's statement of several rescues, including an intoxicated woman who fell off the wharf, a man who ended up on rocks near the rowing club, and two cyclists, one of whom drowned.

"While we're looking at the deaths in the harbour, there's a lot more stories of people falling into the water," Margaret Levings said. "And I don't know whether the council has the true picture of the statistics."

Roberts said he could only comment on the period of time he had been involved with the council and waterfront safety, maintaining all information about the waterfront risk and mitigating unintended falls with balustrades was made available to elected members.

"We took that to council."

Margaret Levings asked whether the council had gone down to the waterfront.

World.title: Auckland commuters may pay up to $7 a trip as congestion charge options revealed
World.content:
Congestion charge may cost up to $7 Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Auckland Councillors have voted to take the next steps with three potential options for congestion charging during peak times.

The three proposed time-of-use charging schemes were predicted to reduce peak time congestion by anywhere from 2 percent to 13 percent.

One option was to charge commuters entering the city centre during rush hour, while another included city fringe suburbs like Newmarket and Newton, and possibly Ponsonby and Parnell.

A third option would also include core motorways such as from the Harbour Bridge to Point Chevalier and Mount Wellington.

Waitākere Ward councillor Shane Henderson said any charges would need to be balanced with investment in transport alternatives.

Waitākere Ward councillor Shane Henderson. Auckland City Council / Supplied

"In West Auckland that means the northwestern busway will need to be committed to by the government ... because people need proper alternatives."

Henderson said it was important to get Aucklanders feedback on the three proposals.

City Centre Cordon is described as the "fairest, simplest" and "most feasible scheme", saving four minutes of travel time. Supplied / Auckland Council

"We're putting it out to the people, and saying 'what do you think about this?' And we'll go from there."

After the options are confirmed by the Transport and Infrastructure Delivery Committee on Tuesday, initial public consultation will start in mid-November before an option is decided on in 2027.

Council documents described the city centre option as the "fairest, simplest and likely most feasible scheme," but noted it would raise limited revenue to improve public transport.

Charges for this option would be around $3-$4 in the morning peak, and $2-$3 in the afternoon.

The city-fringe option was described as "significantly improved effectiveness compared to the city centre cordon," but noted it would include Auckland Hospital.

Option 2: City Fringe Cordon would charge drivers entering via Newmarket, Newton, Parnell and Ponsonby during peak hours. Supplied / Auckland Council

Charges for this option would be in the order of $5-$6 in the morning peak, and $2-$3 in the afternoon.
